#6114. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#6112. Trump’s ‘invasion’ asylum ban to face justices

The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

“The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition says.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”

Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

#6109. Conservative firebrand Lauren Boebert ousted in Colorado

Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

A newcomer to electoral politics, she quickly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch announced he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

#6107. Report: Lufthansa to Cut 1,000 Jobs

Lufthansa Group plans to lay off around 1,000 full-time workers at its flagship carrier as elevated fuel prices and service disruptions continue to undercut earnings.

The airline group disclosed the cuts in a letter sent to employees and seen by Dow Jones Newswire, according to The Wall Street Journal. The reductions will target Lufthansa’s hubs in Frankfurt and Munich.

Company leaders said their 2024 turnaround plan, initially expected to boost earnings by €2.5 billion over four years, is no longer enough to keep the brand on solid financial ground.

“The year 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, the still very high fuel costs, nine days of strike action, and our already very high cost base have intensified the situation,” the letter said.

Lufthansa failed to reach an agreement with its pilot union earlier this week, setting the stage for a possible work stoppage. The impasse has already resulted in two short strikes, one in February, the other in March.

Lufthansa Group has spoken openly about the damage caused by higher fuel prices over the last nine months. Over the summer, it retired aircraft, cut routes, and warned that layoffs were likely unless prices eased.

According to EuroNews, Lufthansa has lost on average about €20 million per month since the start of the year.

#6105. Türkiye Just Announced a New Golden Visa Starting at $150,000

Türkiye is one of the world’s most visited countries, straddling the vibrant crossroads of Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. With sun-soaked Mediterranean beaches, Ottoman-influenced gastronomy, historic mosques, and bustling bazaars, it’s no surprise that the country attracted nearly 64 million visitors in 2025. But if your love of the country has you considering a prolonged vacation (or perhaps a second home), the government’s new golden visa might be a good fit—so long as you have $150,000 to spend.

On November 17, Türkiye's president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan signed a decision to enact a new foreign investor visa. The program offers two pathways: a $150,000 investment for a three-year residence permit, or $200,000 for a five-year stay (both of which can extend to the applicant’s spouse and dependents).

As for where your money goes, you can deposit your funds in a local bank, buy government debt instruments, contribute to a pension plan, or invest in real estate or venture capital funds. No matter which pathway you select, you must hold your investment for at least half the visa term (as in, 1.5 years for the three-year visa or 2.5 years for the five-year visa). That means you could potentially withdraw your investment as early as after 18 months, according to IMI Daily, an investment migration trade publication.

The president’s announcement doesn't detail when or how foreigners can begin to apply, or the specific documents required. However, applications for the country’s other residence-by-investment permits require documents such as proof of financial means and health insurance, according to the government’s Investment and Finance Office.

If you don’t want to shell out $150,000, Türkiye offers other (renewable) relocation pathways. You may qualify for a two-year Short-Term Residence Permit for reasons such as tourism and university-sponsored research. Or, if your spouse is Turkish, you could apply for the three-year Family Residence Permit. Once you’ve lived in the country continuously for eight years, you’ll be eligible to apply for the indefinite Long-Term Residence Permit, which grants you almost all the same perks as citizenship, minus civic duties such as the ability to vote and mandatory military service.

It's important to note that the new golden visa does not provide permanent citizenship. If you’re hoping to find your way into a passport, get ready to spend more. Türkiye’s citizenship-by-investment pipeline will require you to buy a home worth at least $400,000, invest at least $500,000 in sectors such as government bonds or venture capital funds, or, alternatively, help create at least 50 jobs.

Over the last few years, the influx of new residency-by-investment programs has made it easier for wealthy travelers to relocate internationally. In New Zealand, you can invest $1 million New Zealand Dollars (about $567,300) in exchange for a three-year work-to-residency track. For Mediterranean living, Greece offers a five-year permit for a 250,000 euro (about $291,120) investment in a startup. Or, for a more affordable option, Paraguay has a permanent residency program for those who can invest $150,000 in “tourism projects” or $200,000 in stocks or real estate—putting it in line with Türkiye as one of the more affordable relocation options.

#6104. American Airlines Offers “His” Free First Class Upgrade For $91, Then Tells Frequent Flyer To Delete His Complaint

An American Airlines frequent flyer complained about a $91 first class upgrade offer and received a response asking him to delete his post. That might sound like an airline trying to suppress criticism, but there is a much more sensible explanation: his screenshot exposed his reservation details. As for the inexpensive upgrade itself, I see a pragmatic opportunity rather than a scandal.

This hit my algorithm on X (and apparently VFTW too), but an AAdvantage Executive Platinum member took to the platform to express frustration that American was offering paid first class upgrades for $91 while his complimentary upgrade had not cleared (this was on a short 551-mile flight from Dallas to El Paso).

American acknowledged his frustration, then added:

“Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.”

The response attracted attention, but the screenshot included the passenger’s reservation confirmation number. That is a good reason to remove it and not a sign of AA trying to hide from its transactional upgrade policy!

We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we're sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

— americanair (@AmericanAir) November 18, 2026

It seems obvious to me that American was trying to protect the passenger here.

A reservation confirmation number, often called a record locator or PNR, is something you should keep private. Combined with your last name, it can potentially allow someone to retrieve your booking. Depending on the airline and its security controls, that could expose information about your trip or allow someone to interfere with it. At least with AA you also need your birthdate in order to access the record online or on the AA app.

Posting a screenshot to make a point about upgrades should not mean giving strangers an opportunity to tamper with your reservation…and some losers have far too much on their hand (which I’ve found out the hard way and why even when I “live blog” I never truly live blog).

American could have explained this much better. A simple request to remove the screenshot because it contained private booking information would have avoided the ambiguity. The passenger could then have reposted his complaint with those details obscured.

As to the underlying complaint, I understand why an Executive Platinum member would be frustrated. If you have directed substantial business to an airline and are waiting for an upgrade, watching the airline offer that seat for a relatively small payment can feel like your loyalty counts for very little.

But I am not going to attack American for selling inexpensive upgrades. This is the business model now, and I use it to my advantage when I fly AA. If the economy fare is attractive and American subsequently offers a reasonably priced upgrade, I can evaluate the total cost and decide whether first class is worth it. Sometimes it is. Sometimes I am perfectly happy staying where I am, like on a recent flight where I ended up with an entire row to myself. Oddly, sometimes the cost of the upgrade is more than buying the ticket outright…I have no explanation for that.

That is a much more straightforward transaction than spending more throughout the year in the hope that an airline will eventually reward me with a seat it would still prefer to sell.

Fundamentally, a complimentary upgrade that has not cleared, even at the gate, is not a seat that already belongs to the elite member. We can debate all day long about how prominently or aggressively airlines market upgrades when frequent flyers are waiting when upgrades are dangled like a carrot on a stick, but passengers can respond to that change by reconsidering how much they are willing to spend pursuing status.

I am a free agent, and it is liberating. More people should try it. Two years in, I’m more happy than ever (and flying in first class more than ever on domestic flights). I  choose a flight because the schedule works or because the price makes sense, without worrying that I am depriving my preferred airline of another qualifying flight or dollar toward next year’s status.

If American offers a good fare and an inexpensive first class upgrade, great. I can take advantage of it. I do not need to be an Executive Platinum member to recognize a good deal (as much as I miss the oneworld emerald lounge access when traveling internationally).

That does not mean status has become worthless. I still receive occasional complimentary upgrades as both an American Airlines Gold and United Airlines Gold member. I appreciate those upgrades very much, especially when I am not expecting them. But I do not build my travel plans around them. Hoping for a free upgrade seems futile in many cases even with top-tier status, particularly when the airline business model now centers on actively trying to sell the remaining seats.

For me, an occasional upgrade is a pleasant bonus on a flight I was otherwise willing to fly in economy class on. But upgrades are not a compelling reason to keep spending more with one airline when another offers a better flight….sorry, but the value proposition is gone.

American Airlines could have been clearer about why it wanted this passenger to delete his post. Still, the exposed reservation details provide a sensible explanation, and I would not characterize the request as an attempt to silence criticism.

As for the $91 upgrade, I am pragmatically happy those offers exist. They give me another way to sit up front without organizing my travel around the pursuit of top-tier status. I still enjoy the occasional complimentary upgrade, but choosing flights on my own terms, and paying for a better seat when the price is right, has been far more satisfying than chasing an upgrade that may never clear. Try it, you’ll like it.

Dude is an EP, yet instead of taking one of the 14 daily flights between DFW and PHX, he’s connecting in El Paso. Clearly comfort is not his priority. I don’t think he really gets to have an opinion on what AA charges for upgrades.

Maybe he got one of those 6.5K AAdvantage specials! 😉

Before judging perhaps think this through from a practical standpoint.

1. I can’t see his full itinerary. Perhaps it included an overnight in ELP for meetings with a continuation to PHX the next evening? 2. You can sometimes get very attractive fares on non hub connections. I’ve done it myself on many occasions. 3. So what? Flexing is never a good look.

#6102. Review: Air France Business Class Lounge – Paris (CDG) – Terminal 2E, Hall L (Now Sans Sauna…)

You can read a more comprehensive review below, but here are some key points:

I’m big fan of this lounge..it’s a nice one even without the controversial sauna. Here are some photos:

> Read More: Air France Closes Paris Lounge Sauna After Passengers Apparently Turned It Into A Sex Den

Although I’ve been to this lounge several times over the years, my last formal review was when it first opened in 2019, which I’ve included as a point of reference below.

I’ve showcased stock photos of the lounge before, but the photos below are all my own. Because the spa in the La Premiere Lounge closed early, I was offered a spa treatment in this new business class lounge. Although it was in a different section of the terminal, I was driven over and did not have to re-clear security.

The lounge is located on the upper level just past the security checkpoint. As you enter the lounge, you’ll be greeted by a moving sign that resembles a glass of champagne.

Since the purpose of my visit to the lounge was to use the spa, let’s start there. Immediately upon arrival I was ushered into a treatment room and given a 15-minute facial. The lady who performed the facial was chatty and gave me a laundry list of cream recommendations, bluntly stating that my face was too dry. Normally, you can sign up for these treatments on a first-come, first-served basis when you reach the lounge. Advance reservations are not permitted.

This lounge is spread out over one (very) large area with couches and chairs scattered throughout the lounge. Perhaps my visit, on December 23rd, was not a typical Saturday evening, but the lounge was less than 1/4 full. The entire rear half of the lounge was virtually empty.

The lounge manager saw I was taking pictures and knew I was a La Premiere passenger, so he beckoned me to follow him into a room marked “Private”. The room, he explained, was reserved for top-tier elites (by request) or special VIP guests.

In the center of the lounge is a beautiful dining room called Le Balcon with velvet couches and brass accents. It serves as a place to eat and a cocktail bar in the evening.

Buffets are stationed throughout the lounge with a selection of beverages and hot and cold food items.

At the far end of the lounge is an open kitchen in which a special dish of the day is prepared.

With the exception of the cocktail bar, alcohol is self-serve and champagne (Laurent Perrier) is available.

Even more than a facial, I would have loved to use the sauna in this lounge. Sadly, a guest had become ill the day before and vomited in it. Thus, it was quarantined pending sterilization. So much for that idea….

> Read More: A New Airport Lounge With A Sauna

Shower suites and restrooms were also available.

(This is a handicapped shower…they do not all look like this).

Next to the Clarins Spa was a rest area with chairs designed for napping. Don’t forget to set your alarm if you use one of these!

In all honesty, I liked this lounge a lot but liked the decor of the Terminal 2E, Hall M lounge better. The dining area / cocktail bar in the center of this lounge is beautiful. Everything else is just nice. Air France offers excellent lounges in Paris that are worth stopping in at before your flight whether you are flying in business class or simply have SkyTeam elite status. Don’t forget to sign up for a complimentary facial or massage…it is worthwhile.

> Read More: Air France Business Class Lounge Paris (CDG) – Terminal 2E, Hall M

#6100. Former Washington Rep. Jim McDermott dies at 89

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call)

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

“Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”

When McDermott announced his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”

Born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

He attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a new life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

“I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”

As he said, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

Then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

McDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

“Jim McDermott was as big as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”

#6099. Delta Air Lines New-Hire Pilot Reportedly Fired After Answering His Cellphone While Taxiing

A new-hire Delta Air Lines pilot reportedly answered his cellphone while taxiing for departure, prompting the captain to return to the gate and have him removed. According to an account shared on the Black Box Aviation Podcast, the first officer subsequently lost his job. If accurate, this was a remarkably poor way to begin an airline career at Delta!

The story comes from the Black Box Aviation Podcast, which recently discussed distractions on the flight deck and the consequences of using personal phones while working.

According to the account, a Delta first officer was undergoing Initial Operating Experience, or IOE, when he answered his cellphone while the aircraft was taxiing for departure. Rather than continue to the runway, the captain returned to the gate. The first officer was removed and reportedly fired.

IOE involves flying actual airline trips under the supervision of a check pilot. A new hire may have substantial flying experience elsewhere, but is still learning how to apply the new airline’s procedures in everyday operations.

https://twitter.com/the_black_box01/status/2122695070885290294

There are limitations to this account. I have not obtained confirmation from Delta (understandably, no response). Furthermore, no flight number or date was referenced, so the recent discussion does not necessarily imply that this just happened. The reported dismissal should be understood as the podcast’s account…and incidents like this have been part of airline pilot lore in online forums for many years.

I suspect some passengers might hear this story and think firing someone over a phone call sounds excessive. After all, the airplane was still on the ground.

But taxiing requires the attention of both pilots. A captain may be steering, but the first officer still has work to do, including monitoring the aircraft’s progress and air traffic control instructions. A wrong turn or missed runway instruction can have very serious consequences…being a pilot is one of the professions that leaves no room for error.

The federal sterile cockpit rule specifically includes taxi among the critical phases of flight. It prohibits activities that could distract flight crew members from their duties.

A separate provision restricts the use of personal wireless communications devices at a flight crew duty station during flight, with exceptions for specified purposes under approved airline procedures. The FAA’s guidance makes clear that prohibited personal use includes telephone conversations, texting, and browsing the internet.

Pilots can use approved electronic flight bags (EFBs are the iPads that replace paper manuals and charts) and make necessary operational communications. Taking an ordinary personal call while taxiing is another matter.

I spend far too much time on my phone, as my weekly screen time reports reminds me every Sunday morning. I understand how reflexively we reach for it when it rings or lights up. But there are times when it simply needs to remain put away, and working in the cockpit of a moving passenger jet is certainly one of them.

What strikes me about this account is the setting. This was reportedly a new hire being supervised during training. That should be a time to demonstrate that you understand the procedures and can be trusted to follow them!

If the account is complete and the call was personal, I understand why the captain would have concerns about continuing the flight with that first officer. Returning to the gate would inconvenience passengers, but I would rather be delayed than have a captain continue after losing confidence in the person beside him.

The employment decision is harder to assess without the full record. We do not know whether there were previous concerns or what explanation the first officer offered. I tend to be more forgiving and don’t think that every mistake during training should end a career. Even so, this would be a serious lapse in judgment. A pilot arriving at Delta should already understand why answering a personal call during taxi is unacceptable.

The Black Box Aviation Podcast recounts a Delta new-hire first officer answering his cellphone during taxi, being removed after a return to the gate, and subsequently losing his job. The incident remains unconfirmed beyond that account.

If it happened as described, I understand the captain’s decision. Passengers should be able to expect both pilots to give their attention to operating the aircraft safely. Answering personal phone call is unacceptable.

image: Delta file photo. (Those pictured are not connected to this alleged incident)

#6097. American Plans Return to Israel, Partners With Israir

After a three-year hiatus, American Airlines is preparing to resume service to Israel.

The carrier said Friday that it will restart flights from New York-JFK to Tel Aviv on March 27, 2027. Flights will operate daily using Boeing 777-200ER aircraft.

American has not flown to Israel since the Hamas attack on southern Israel in October 2023. It remained on the sidelines even as rivals United and Delta resumed service to Ben Gurion International Airport, though they too were forced to temporarily pause flights during fighting between Israel and Iran.

Israeli officials had questioned why American was slow to reconnect the country, citing the importance of air links between Tel Aviv and New York. The airline did not offer an explanation beyond concern for the safety of its passengers and crew.

American also said Friday that it has formed a commercial partnership with Tel Aviv-based low-cost carrier Israir. The agreement will expand in phases over time, American said; in the first phase, Israir will place its code on American’s flights between JFK and Tel Aviv.

The carriers will also work to implement an interline agreement that would give Israir customers access to American’s network across the U.S., Canada, Latin America, and the Caribbean from JFK.

“American looks forward to building a relationship with Israir that will give customers the convenient, well-connected travel options they desire,” American Senior Vice President of Alliances Anmol Bhargava said in a news release. “As we prepare to resume service between New York and Tel Aviv next spring, this partnership will help us deliver a stronger customer proposition in the market and create more opportunities for Israir’s travelers to connect beyond our JFK gateway.”

Israir operates five weekly flights between JFK and Tel Aviv using Airbus A330-200 aircraft. New York is its only U.S. destination; most of its network is concentrated in the Near East and Europe.

#6096. Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from new software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin said “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

“We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work."

Thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications."

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment."

Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

The 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

The committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a new one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

“Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell said.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and said their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

At issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have said they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

#6095. Which AI Bots Can Help You Book Travel?

A multitude of new start ups promise AI assistants will “handle your travel.” I’m skeptical of anything that promises to handle my travel, mostly because I’ve spent years learning exactly where airline websites like to hide the landmines and sharing it with our audience. But following Kirby’s (United’s) statement that AI bots would be blocked from its sites, I got curious about where we are with airlines and bots. I wanted to see what happens when an AI agent, one that drives a real web browser the way you or I would (in this case, Grok as ChatGPT, and Claude work differently), sits down at the airline’s own website and tries to book a real itinerary.

To be clear, this is not a test of chatbots that spit out a list of flights and then send you off to do the work yourself. The question here is narrower and more practical. Can an agentic AI search, pick a fare, fill in the forms and get a family of four to the payment page without a human bailing it out? And just as interesting, which airlines let it in the door at all? For this hypothesis, I presumed United would be a certain “no” but what about the others?

I gave the a Grok Bot (a single AI agent) the same basic trip on every airline: Pittsburgh (PIT) to Fort Myers (RSW), one way, on Tuesday, December 15, 2026, for four adults. On American, I used a real award rebooking for my own family while signed in to my AAdvantage account. On Delta, United and Southwest, the agent shopped cash fares while signed out. Grok is unique in two ways, first that it has its “own computer” where it runs your searches instead of yours, and second, that it can securely store your login credentials and operate as you would but it never sees those credentials (don’t ask me how.) I understand that Muse may have some of the same features, but my setup experience there was not as straight forward and I don’t need a fifth AI tool even if it’s integrated into my existing Instagram and Facebook accounts.

I drew one firm line. The agent could go as far as the passenger or payment page, but nothing got purchased in any of these tests. Card details, CVVs and the final “Purchase” click stayed with me and I never processed any of them.

American was the most realistic test and also the most frustrating. The agent had no trouble with the award search on aa.com using my account logged in. It pulled up 40 results for PIT to RSW, with Main Cabin at 10,500 miles one way per person and First at 25,500 miles.

It found AA 3030 acceptable flights from Pittsburgh to Charlotte, connecting to Fort Myers, in Main Cabin for 42,000 miles plus $22.40 for all four of us. If I wanted to, I could train the AI to understand whether I would want a morning or evening flight typically, an acceptable layover range, it could look at my schedule and ensure that we have sufficient time to get to a meeting and work around my schedule and preferences, not just my price. This test didn’t need all of that.

It got that itinerary all the way to “Review and pay.” Then the friction started. My saved card on the account required the CVV to be entered again, which the agent could not supply (and, frankly, should not have). While that was being sorted out, the checkout session expired.

When the agent rebuilt the cart, aa.com threw up its “Please confirm you’re a human” challenge with an “I’m not a robot” box. The AI dutifully lied but identified where and how that was running. That page comes from a bot manager, which assigns every visitor a score from human to bot and can raise that score as the same visitor keeps making requests. Rebuilding a cart several times looks automated (because it was.) At that point a human had to step in.

I’d rate this as a 90% solution with a final human check and ultimate purchase as the last 10% to complete. This is likely a best case scenario to keep control of your miles or money and ensure what you book is correct.

Delta was the cleanest run of the bunch. The agent set up the one-way search, added four passengers, picked the date and landed on a results page with flights connecting in Atlanta and arriving after 9pm, at $192 per person in Main because this one was not a logged in redemption.

From there it handled the Basic vs Main Classic choice, clicked past the upsell screens (an airline’s worst nightmare) and reached “Review and Pay” with a trip total of just under $965 for four in Main Classic. No captcha, no “are you human”, nothing. If Delta’s site was suspicious of my agent, it did not show it. There was no resistance. I flag this as an advantage for Delta, because tech forward clients will love that they can get an entire booking done start to finish without their intervention.

United, like Delta, also let the agent through to the end of my test, but it took more attempts. The date field was finicky, with the calendar jumping ahead to January and February 2027 before the agent got back to December as I watched it work. The travelers dialog took several retries before it stopped saying “1 Adult” and accepted four. Not as smooth as Delta, but not a total block which I would have thought they’d install.

Once the search ran, the agent took the first result (which it did not do for the others) a 6 AM departure via Washington Dulles, and correctly skipped Basic Economy (United makes you tick a “Basic Economy works for me” box first) in favor of the Standard fare. That is a reasonable choice for a family, but my kids would have something to say about a 6 AM departure, which is a good reminder that an AI agent only knows the preferences you give it.

It then reached the “Traveler Info” page with a total of $964.80, which is, amusingly (but from a competitive standpoint, unsurprising), the exact same total Delta showed for four people. No captcha appeared on United at any point.

Southwest ended up with the best itinerary and the lowest price. The first result was a nonstop leaving Pittsburgh at 9:50 AM and arriving in Fort Myers at 12:30 PM. The agent chose the Choice fare at $222 per person, for a total of $885.60 for four. If it only it knew my kids, this nonstop would be the clear winner even if the price wasn’t better than United and Delta. That said, I would also need to input information about what’s preferred when comparing miles and points, and my personal valuation so that it doesn’t choose even an $885 one-way for four people if American happened to be running 5,000-mile one-ways.

The site itself was the slowest of the four. The “Continue” button took its time to respond, and a “Log in for faster checkout” pop-up appeared before the agent could choose to continue as a guest. Had I logged in, my results may have been different and there’s a case for storing all of these logins in its “vault.” Then again, with the recent spat of compromised technical systems worldwide – there’s also very much a case for not storing all of my logins either.

Still, it got to the “Passengers” page, step 2 of 5, without any bot restrictions.

This isn’t an entirely comprehensively list as not all of them were useful for both the Live And Let’s Fly audience as well as my purposes. But what I did do is ask the AI to check whether each airline has its own AI assistants that can actually search, book, change or cancel a flight, or whether those tools just answer FAQs and hand you to a person.

Alaska is the one that has built something close to a trip-planning AI. Its “Trip inspiration with AI” tool, Alaska Inspires, sits in the Book menu on alaskaair.com. Alaska and Microsoft (I suspect an even further neutered version of Co-Pilot) say you can type or speak a request in plain language, get destination ideas, and discover, compare and book in the same flow. In a March 2025 interview, Alaska’s director of innovation, Bernadette Berger, gave examples like “Where can I go in Europe for under 80k miles?” Microsoft’s write-up claims a 7% conversion rate versus 5% for the standard booking widget. My AI was not able to run my booking through Inspires so this would be a failure in my experience but I am willing to try again using different parameters.

JetBlue does have a customer-service AI but I was unsuccessful in attempting to advance it further.

Breeze Airways has gone further on digital customer care than most low-cost carriers. VP of Guest Experience Danny Cox, says Breeze uses Gladly’s generative “Answer Threads” tool to present change and cancellation options in chat or SMS, and that AI fully resolves 37% of conversations. That is post-booking help, not a bot that will shop a new itinerary for you. Breeze’s own contact pages blocked my lookup, so I could not independently confirm how the current chat or text flow works for a brand-new booking. That would be a failure but again, I suspect a logged in account might perform better.

Allegiant does put a bot on its site but this is for customer service alone. Sun Country and JSX are even thinner on the consumer-facing side and my bot failed for all of these carriers too.

On the cash side, AI agents can already do the boring part of booking. All three cash bookings reached a passenger or payment page, and none of them hit a captcha. The agent picked sensible fares, navigated upsell screens and dealt with clunky widgets on its own, even if United’s date picker and Southwest’s sluggish buttons cost it some time. Adding that personal context could make this a very practical option.

The real wall is at the end. Payment details, CVVs and timed checkout sessions are designed to need a human, and I think that is fine. The bigger issue is bot detection because it wasn’t really built to detect or negate AI bots but general hacks that could operate massive attacks on the sites. American is the airline that blocked my agent outright, and it happened on the most complex booking of the test, involving award miles and a signed-in account. Whether that was because of the account, the repeated cart rebuilds or just AA’s settings that day, the result was the same.

But United is the only one that has said it won’t allow AI bots and absolutely did.

Out of all of the tests, Delta was the easiest and had me most encouraged, while United and Southwest made it harder but not impossible and not specifically against AI, just the design of the site. American was the only one that really made it difficult and that shocked me. This test, and travelers using these tools for booking purposes are narrow at the moment but as AI agents/bots continue to advance and become normalized, the carriers will likely do something more robust. That said, there could be a strong advantage for those that are “AI-friendly.” Competitive markets like Los Angeles and New York might see more flights sold on Delta from indifferent travelers solely because it’s easier. The real question becomes how comfortable the general public becomes and with that, hopefully not too comfortable or websites will crash from users searching flights hundreds of times a day.

What do you think? Would you store your logins? Would you entrust an AI bot or agent to return travel results for you even if you have to complete the purchase on your own?

Join our mailing list for a daily summary of posts! We never sell your info.

Kyle is a freelance travel writer with contributions to Time, the Washington Post, MSNBC, Yahoo!, Reuters, Huffington Post, Travel Codex, PenAndPassports, Live And Lets Fly and many other media outlets. He is also co-founder of Scottandthomas.com, a travel agency that delivers "Travel Personalized." He focuses on using miles and points to provide a premium experience for his wife, daughter, and son. #6094. Early Travel Tuesday Deals Are in Motion—Save on Bookings With Expedia, Hyatt, and Celebrity Today

If there's one thing better than having a vacation on the calendar, it's knowing you didn’t pay full price for it. And right on cue, one of the most exciting stretches of the travel-booking year is kicking off. With Thanksgiving around the corner, Travel Tuesday is already making its presence known, bringing early-bird deals on flights, hotels, cruises, and vacation packages for travelers ready to trade their wish lists for boarding passes.

The annual event, which falls on the Tuesday after Thanksgiving—this year, on December 1—has become a prime moment for savvy travelers to score booking discounts, whether that’s a Caribbean beach escape in the depths of winter, a European summer adventure, or simply a long weekend somewhere new.

The best part? You don't have to wait until the official Travel Tuesday date to start saving. Airlines and hotel groups are getting a head start with early promotions, and some of the most appealing offers—from top-rated cruise lines to flight fares—are already live. I've rounded up nine of the best early Travel Tuesday deals worth booking, or at the very least keeping an eye on as more are announced.

World of Hyatt has already dropped its annual Cyber Sale, slashing rates by up to 25% for its members across more than 1,250 hotels and luxury resorts across the globe. With a travel window stretching all the way through April 30, 2027, you have plenty of runway to lock in trips from a sun-drenched winter escape to a spring break getaway—or that bucket-list vacation you’ve been putting off. If you’re not a member yet, the sale is open to the general public for up to 20% off. (That said, signing up takes two seconds and is totally free, so don’t leave the money on the table!) Just make sure to lock in your dates by December 8, 2026.

Save on Sandals Saint Vincent and The Grenadines—the perfect sanctuary for relaxation within over 50 acres of breathtaking Jurassic Park–like scenery.

Want the best bang for your buck in the Caribbean? Sister brands Sandals and Beaches have you covered. The early Travel Tuesday deals from these all-inclusives ensure up to $750 in air credits to help offset flight costs, alongside up to 65% off hotels and resorts across the entire resort portfolio—from Grenada to St. Lucia, Saint Vincent and The Grenadines, Curaçao, and beyond.

Select bookings promise some exclusive perks too: At Sandals Resorts specifically, travelers can receive up to $2,250 on booking and spa credits to use during their adults-only stay. Families booking Beaches Turks and Caicos (including the new Treasure Beach Village) or Beaches Negril in Jamaica can receive up to $1,650 in booking and spa credits. Just book by Travel Tuesday itself for qualifying travel through December 31, 2028.

Whether you’re an avid traveler or not, there’s a high chance you’ve booked a flight, hotel, or rental on Expedia. Lucky for you, now just so happens to be the site’s biggest sale of the year, with savings on family beach resorts, romantic getaways, cabin retreats, and everywhere in between. If you’ve already got a special destination in mind, simply enter your city of choice and travel dates into the website or app’s search bar, use filters to refine your search, and see which Travel Tuesday deals come rolling in. Up until December 3, those ready to book via Expedia can save up to 50% on stays in cities all over the world—plus, onboard perks on select cruises, eligible discounts on car rentals, and more.

In true holiday spirit, the ever-luxe and tropical hotel group Sun Siyam is offering up to 50% in savings across its six stunning resorts, from secluded barefoot hideaways in the Maldives to lush, high-end retreats in Sri Lanka. The timely sale allows for bookings made before November 30, and for eligible stays through October 31, 2027, depending on the property. Need more incentive to stay at Sun Siyam other than a discount at its fabulous locations? Easy—these stays come with memorable perks, like complimentary seaplane transfers, spa treatments, floating breakfasts, excursions, water sports, and dining experiences galore.

At Siyam World, for one, guests can save up to 50% while enjoying an all-inclusive meal plan. Meanwhile, at Sun Siyam Olhuveli, guests can receive 50% off airport transfers, 30% off à la carte dining, 25% off spa treatments, and 20% off water sports, with complimentary sunset cruises on qualifying stays. And there’s way more where that came from.

It’s not often we find a “someday” trip at such a tempting price—but an early Travel Tuesday deal from Quark Expeditions puts that dream getaway well within reach. For those dreaming of the ends of the Earth, the cruise line is offering savings of up to 40% on select Arctic and Antarctic voyages. Available to book now through December 3, the limited-time promotion brings the world’s most exclusive polar frontiers within closer reach—from the icy wilderness of the Antarctic Peninsula and Svalbard to the rugged landscapes of Patagonia, Greenland, Iceland, and beyond. And yes, bucket-list itineraries—including the time-saving Antarctic Express: Fly the Drake—are also part of the offer.

Celebrity is launching this stunning river ship in summer 2027—and you can sail it for the best booking value yet.

Looking for a value-forward river cruise in picture-perfect corners of Europe? Top-rated cruise line Celebrity Cruises is releasing a set of flash sales over the next week, with its latest being a discount on exactly that—and the perks are pretty enticing. For one, if you book before November 24, you can save 75% on a second guest’s fare on sweet river sailings, from the Danube River to see Vienna and Budapest or venturing from Brussels to Amsterdam on a hunt for tulips. There are also select sailings—including a New Year’s cruise on the Rhine River—where you can save up to $1,000 in air credit per person.

When it comes to savvy ways to fly, it’s no secret that Skyscanner provides heaps of flight options and routes where value is front and center. If you’re looking to score cheap Travel Tuesday flights, you can count on the site for price drops on airfare over the next week through Cyber Monday. Along with vacation packages, hotel deals (at up to 35% off), and an app for price tracking, the Skyscanner website has an entire guide on and around Travel Tuesday itself—from advice on reducing fees to using shared loyalty points and beyond.

Whether you are mapping out a holiday road trip or chasing winter sun, scoring the right car rental deal is half the adventure. While highly regarded car rental company Avis has not yet rolled out an official Travel Tuesday promotion ahead of the December 1 event, you won’t have to wait to lock in some stellar savings. Right now, you can trim up to 35% off base rates simply by choosing the Pay Now option online, or unlock up to 30% off with Avis’s current discount code AWD S169100.

Book a discounted tour to the cloud forests of Costa Rica.

If you’ve got a sudden urge to get up and go, this is G Adventures’s biggest sale of the year—and it includes hundreds of early Travel Tuesday deals with up to 30% off tours and experiences across the globe. With some trips departing in the next 60 days, we’re talking discounts on some of the group’s most-loved and top-rated trips, including Thailand Island Hopping on the West Coast and chasing Costa Rica: Coastlines and Clouds Forests. If your schedule’s flexible and your passport’s ready, this is the kind of spontaneous deal you jump on before it disappears.

#6093. Review: Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres (Hyatt Inclusive)

Of note, I was in Cancun, Mexico for business meetings at another resort but wanted to evaluate both this experience for our readers as well as the overall position of Hyatt in its ever-growing Inclusives collection. My stay was almost exactly 24 hours and solo which is uncharacteristic at this destination resort. My experience will likely differ from other guests due to those factors.

Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres is an adults-only resort in the Hyatt Inclusive Collection, and I toured it on a site visit in November 2026. It sits on a stretch of white-sand beach in Costa Mujeres, 12 miles north of Cancun. Cancun International Airport is the arrival airport. I could not confirm a single official transfer time from the property page. Tour listings commonly put the drive in a 30 to 45 minute range.

Address: Carretera Punta Sam – Isla Blanca, Mz 2, Lt 10, Costa Mujeres, Zona Continental Isla Mujeres, Quintana Roo 77400, Mexico

Google Maps: Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres

Hyatt is the best in the business at high end resort arrivals. I had given my name at the security gate and by the time I reached the lobby, the door to the vehicle was opened for me, I was greeted by name and a “welcome home”, a constant refrain throughout my stay. It’s a small thing and maybe cliché but it was effective. I was given a Globalist upgrade even though rules at all-inclusives differ from the rest of the chain. As my upgrade was in a Preferred room, I was brought into a private room at the front of the lobby where check-in was done for me.

The lobby is an open-air room under an arched woven ceiling, with a direct view out to the ocean.

The resort is spread across 10 buildings with 505 keys. Of those, 221 are Preferred Club keys with an elevated experience. My building (and others like it) had just five rooms on each floor and just five floors which made it feel boutique rather than massive. Every oceanfront room is Preferred Club, and so are the first two buildings on either side.

The room views follow a simple rule by floor. Every first floor room is a swim-out, floors two through four are tropical view, and the fifth floor is ocean view or ocean front. That makes booking easy to reason through: if you want to step off your patio into the water, go low, and if you want the sea, go high.

The walkways give a sense of grandeur and space. All of the flora is local, and in a touch I loved, the service rooms are named after the plants.

There are four pools, and each one has a unique characteristic. The Jungle pool is drinks only and hidden in the middle of the resort by trees. The Social pool runs activities throughout the day at this adults-only resort for those who want to participate. There is also an infinity pool on the edge of the beach, and then the Preferred Club pool for those staying in that category. These are separate from the first floor swim-outs.

The spa (hydrotherapy is included for Preferred guests) featured an outdoor circuit that included both hot and cold plunge pools, amongst other therapeutic services.

The Preferred Club pool was the most frequented, though some images below look more vacant due to rain that rolled through during my opportunity to collect media on my short stay.

The gym is open to every guest from 6 AM to 8 PM, and it is outfitted with Technogym equipment.

The spa is open 8 AM to 8 PM with 17 treatment cabins and a beauty salon, and hydrotherapy is included. That last part is the headline. The hydrotherapy space is ridiculous, easily the standout of the entire property for me, and it is the kind of amenity that would make me pick this resort over a competitor down the beach. There are indoor and outdoor showers as well.

The men’s changing room featured private showers with an option for indoor or outdoor experiences.

The theater seats 264 people and hosts cabaret and Mayan shows. There are also pickleball courts, which I am starting to think should be required equipment at any resort that wants a younger crowd as well as padel for the European set (and growing American interest.)

Secrets is an adults-only brand, and every room here comes with what the company calls Unlimited-Luxury. For a standard guest that means unlimited dining and top-shelf drinks, Wi-Fi, daytime activities and nightly entertainment, with tips and taxes included. Add 24-hour room service, a mini-bar refreshed daily (you can ask for just about anything you want in there), and pool and beach wait service for all guests.

The Preferred Club is an upgrade, and at this resort it is a big one because it owns the oceanfront. Secrets lists personalized check-in and check-out, afternoon hot and cold hors d’oeuvres, desserts and premium liquors, access to the Preferred Club lounge and beach bar, an upgraded mini-bar, upgraded bath amenities, butler service, Bali beds at the pool and beach reserved for club guests, and exclusive dining at the Preferred Club beach restaurant. Preferred also gives club guests exclusive access to an infinity pool and puts an oversized soaking tub on the terrace of the upgraded suites (at least with the oceanfronts).

I book a lot of Hyatt’s all-inclusives through Hyatt Privé rates, and this resort is one of 388 in the collection. Privé is Hyatt’s invitation-only program for travel advisors, so you only get the benefits when an approved advisor makes the booking, and the stay still earns World of Hyatt points and elite nights.

The all-inclusive version of Privé looks a lot different from a Park Hyatt booking. As I wrote when Hyatt’s all-inclusive resorts joined Privé, there is no room upgrade and no breakfast benefit, since every meal is already included. At this property, Privé guests receive a $100 resort credit per stay, a welcome amenity and letter, hydrotherapy access, and early check-in and late check-out based on availability.

Elite status matters here more than at most all-inclusives. Under World of Hyatt’s terms, Globalists get the best room available at check-in, including rooms with club access, at the resort’s discretion. Explorists are eligible for upgrades too, but not to standard suites or club rooms. Travelers who have stayed at Secrets resorts as Globalists report being designated Preferred Club guests even when they did not land in a club building, which unlocks the lounge, pool and beach areas. This was my experience on all accounts at the resort. Late checkout is 2 PM for Explorists and 4 PM for Globalists, subject to availability at resorts. It was able to honor my request for a late check-out, I did not arrive early enough to request the early check-in. Hyatt waives resort fees on eligible paid rates (at least for now) and award nights for Globalists, and on award nights only for every other tier, and Globalists also get free parking on free nights though in 2028 Globalists will have to select this as a preference. One catch is that Suite Upgrade Awards cannot be used at Secrets resorts, so you cannot lock in a suite with one here.

Weddings are big business here. The courtyard outside the theater is the setting, with the sunset behind it, and the resort hosts lots of them. The resort disclosed its occupancy to me but it wasn’t clear if it was for public consumption. It was shockingly high especially for a Thursday in mid-November. Over the holidays or spring break all the hotels are full but this is a period where I would have expected a lull. Still, despite being extremely full, it never felt crowded.

For meetings and groups, the convention space measures 9,800 square feet and splits into five sections. The boardroom was occupied at the time so I couldn’t include images of that.

Restaurants can be booked in advance through the Hyatt Inclusive Collection app, which I wish more all-inclusives offered. Nobody wants to find out at 7 PM that the restaurant they wanted is full and through the app this can be done well in advance of a guest’s arrival. The dress code in the restaurants is resort casual, though the patio does not require slacks and closed toed shoes for men, shorts are acceptable outside.

The restaurants include: Portofino (Italian), Bordeaux (French), Himitsu (pan-Asian, with sushi and teppanyaki), Oceana (seafood in an open-air setting), Barefoot Grill (light lunch), Market Café (the international buffet, which I noted on site as the Marketplace), Seaside Grill (a poolside grill), and Coco Café. The bars on that list include Rendezvous in the lobby, Barracuda on the beach, a swim-up bar, a beach bar, and the Preferred Club beach bar and lounge bar. There’s also a Sports Bar and Lounge next to the theater.

Oceana is the seafood restaurant, set in an open-air dining room with woven pendant lamps, macrame hangings and a pebble mosaic floor. I chose this for my one dinner on property during my brief stay.

I started with the lamb croquettes, which the menu serves with yogurt and sweet chili sauce, cashews, watercress and a pickled shallot salad, and the Iberian salad with fresh mozzarella, prosciutto, rucula, toasted pistachios, balsamic and roasted peach. A crusty loaf came with the meal.

For a main I had the coconut shrimp, served with parsley orzo pasta, coconut sauce and parmesan crispy, and finished with the mango cheesecake, which the menu plates with vanilla cream and a mango compote with honey and basil.

Market Café, the international buffet I noted as the Marketplace, serves breakfast until 11:30 AM. [TO CONFIRM: lunch and dinner service at Market Café]

Seaside Grill hosts the Preferred Club à la carte breakfast. The official dining page says breakfast there is served for Preferred Club guests only. I tried a number of dishes for lunch to report to our fine audience.

Rendezvous sits at the heart of the property with 360-degree access, so you can walk up to it from any direction.

Preferred Club guests get their own bar at the beach, and the Preferred Club lounge also has an indoor lounge for when the sun gets to be too much.

My room was a Preferred Oceanfront King, a single open room with a king bed against a macrame headboard wall, rattan pendant lights, a ceiling fan, and a daybed sofa facing a marble bistro table. The balcony with jacuzzi looks straight over the beach. In the bathroom, a freestanding tub sits under a wood-slat ceiling beside a walk-in rain shower with a pebble floor and a bench. The double vanity has vessel sinks, round mirrors and a wave-textured wall, and the shower is stocked with Le Labo Bergamote 22 shampoo, conditioner and shower gel. Le Labo is a confirmed winner for me.

I also had the chance to tour a master suites, all of which are oceanfront, and they are also available as swim-outs.

Every first floor room is a swim-out, opening onto the pool.

Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres is an incredible resort that somehow felt small when you were in your building but big enough to have everything. For my stay, I used 45,000 points on a no-notice booking to offset a $1,300/night stay. I have seen rates from $560 for off-season which is without question worth it. I loved the property and I look forward to returning with more time and my wife, but the adults-only nature of the property will make it a harder stay for us to achieve.

What do you think? Have you stayed at Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres?

#6090. Where Was 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Filmed? Behind the Scenes in Spain and Germany

On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we take a look at The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

We’re heading back to Panem for the sixth time this autumn, as the latest Hunger Games prequel hits screens. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the action of the first film and tells the origin story of Katniss Everdeen’s grumpy tutor, Haymitch Abernathy, as he enters the Games himself.

Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy and Whitney Peak as Lenore Dove Baird

Based on the books by Suzanne Collins, the dystopian series is set in a futuristic America in which each district must send a teenage tribute to fight to the death in an annual competition—the idea being that, by doing so, the public will be too afraid to rebel against President Snow.

This edition of the games is known as the Quarter Quell, with double the number of tributes being sent into the arena, meaning the stakes are so much higher. Interest in the film is high, not least because Haymitch is so beloved in the original series, portrayed by Woody Harrelson. Newcomer Joseph Zada takes the lead role in the latest film, while Hollywood heavyweights Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Elle Fanning, and Kieran Culkin also star.

One of the most important sets in the film is the arena where the games take place, and for this, director Francis Lawrence opted not for CGI and a green screen, but instead a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in northern Spain. Below, we look into the locations used in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

Ben Wang as Wyatt Callow, Percy Daggs IV as Ampert Latier, Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy, and Mckenna Grace as Maysilee Donner in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

Within the book and film series, the settings for the Hunger Games are always known to be virtually spectacular. For this film, filmmakers settled on the vast and untouched landscape of Somiedo Natural Park in the Asturias region of northern Spain, which boasts mountain ranges, glacial valleys, beautiful meadows, dense forests, and tranquil lakes. The remote region is also home to the last brown bear population in Europe.

When the tributes are launched into the arena, they are presented with a vast Cornucopia, a pile of weapons, food, and other supplies that might be useful to them in the competition. These scenes were filmed at Somiedo Natural Park, with the Asturian mountains and a glacial lake in the background.

“Somiedo is a spectacular place,” said Pedro Aráez, supervising location manager. “The valleys, forests, and mountains have a very wild, untouched feeling, which was exactly what the filmmakers were looking for. It’s remote, dramatic, and visually unique. When you arrive there, you immediately understand why it was chosen.”

Located close to Somiedo, the Teverga beech forest, Hayedo de Montegrande, was used for some of the dense woodland scenes, in which contestants battle it out and hide in the woods. Other scenes filmed here utilized a series of glacial lakes, the Saliencia Lakes and the Lago de la Cueva.

Iris Apatow as Proserpina Trinket and Elle Fanning as Effie Trinket in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

Before the tributes are launched into the arena, they are first held in special little pods underground which are arranged in a circle around the Cornucopia. The perfect location for this? A velodrome, of course, which is steeply circular so cyclists can race around it. The film crew utilized Berlin’s Velodrom for this very purpose, with its cold, clinical silver decor perfect for matching the hi-tech aesthetic associated with the Capitol.

Prior to entering the Games, tributes must introduce themselves on the public stage, during a televised grand chariot parade in the Capitol. Another Berlin location with links to the sporting world was used for this purpose: the Olympiastadion. For fans of the earlier films, this is the moment when Jennifer Lawrence’s character Katniss becomes “the girl on fire” with her incredible flaming dress.

The futuristic architecture of Edificio Calatrava in Oviedo, Spain—with its striking, claw-like structure—stands in for a building in the Capitol, where President Snow and his government live. The complex was designed by Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava, whose work is known for resembling living organisms. Meanwhile, the 14th-century Ehreshoven Castle, just outside of Cologne, was also used as a filming location, with local press reporting that its lush interiors might have been used to stand in for somewhere inside the Capitol.

A former smelting factory complex in western Germany, Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord provides the backdrop for one of the most atmospheric settings in the films, Haymitch’s home of District 12. The vast complex is able to stand in for multiple places within the district, a former mining town that has fallen on seriously bad times. Rather than being a desolate area stumbled upon by the filmmakers, Landschaftspark is popular for its nightly light installation by British artist Jonathan Park. There are also regular al fresco events here, from film screenings to the annual art-meets-sport Ruhr Games and Traumzeit Festival. Another location in Germany, Lindlar Quarry, was used for District 12, with wooden huts built here to resemble the outskirts of the village.
