#6056. Traveling This Thanksgiving? Here’s the Latest on Flight Delays Following Delta Outage

On Sunday, November 22, US travelers faced another wave of significant flight disruptions ahead of Thanksgiving.

This time around, the issues occurred at the nation’s busiest hub, Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport (ATL), where Delta Air Lines delayed hundreds of flights due to a problem with a critical piece of technology.

The delays sent ripple effects throughout the carrier's US network, snarling travel plans for thousands of Delta fliers heading out on Thanksgiving trips. While the issue was resolved Sunday afternoon, the airline delayed 300 flights and canceled 92 flights on Monday morning, according to FlightAware. “Operations are stable today with automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations fully restored,” a Delta spokesperson told Traveler on Monday. “Delta teams are focused on keeping the operation moving safely and caring for our customers.”

For US travelers, the timing is particularly stressful. AAA projects 5.96 million travelers will take domestic flights over the Thanksgiving holiday period. Plus, Delta’s operational difficulties came only nine days after the FAA declared a rare nationwide ground stop on November 13 that lasted more than four hours and led to multiple days of travel chaos.

While Delta’s technology issues had nothing to do with the FAA systems, both incidents have travelers questioning if their Thanksgiving travel plans will be disrupted. Here’s a look at the current situation and what travelers should know before heading to the airport this week.

This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

On Sunday morning, Delta began having issues with its weight and balance automation system at the Atlanta airport. The system’s critical equipment assesses whether aircraft are too heavy to fly before takeoff.

While the system was out, Delta crews use manual backup processes to help flights depart. However, the technology outage still led to thousands of delays and hundreds of cancellations.

Delta had 2,194 flight delays on November 22, which is about 64% of its schedule, according to FlightAware data. The carrier also had 274 canceled flights on Sunday. Although some of those disruptions were due to other issues, like bad weather in the Northeast, Delta said that 70% of the flight changes were caused by the ATL equipment problems, according to CNN.

The airline said it had restored the system by Sunday afternoon. By Monday morning, Delta’s flight schedules across the country appeared to be getting back on track. However, as of 11 a.m. ET on Monday, the carrier had accumulated more than 300 flight delays and 92 cancellations, FlightAware showed. Now that the technology issue has been resolved, travelers can expect Delta's flight schedule to progressively return to normal but should still prepare for lingering delays through Tuesday, November 24.

Travelers with canceled flights can ask for a full cash refund if they no longer wish to travel. The carrier doesn’t charge passengers to change their flights if they’re booked in any fare class except basic economy (although a difference in fare may apply).

Passengers should continue to check with Delta for the latest information on their flight status. When traveling for Thanksgiving, err on the side of caution and plan to arrive at the airport early: at least two hours before a domestic flight and three hours before an international one.

The ground stop on November 13 was due to a separate issue with air traffic control equipment outages and the telecommunications systems that the FAA uses to track and communicate with planes while they’re flying. “The ground stop was issued out of an abundance of caution,” says the FAA’s statement. “Safety is, and will always remain, the FAA’s highest priority. We will never compromise the safety of the flying public.”

On November 13, the FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was updating telecommunications equipment at an FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, when the issues began, according to the FAA. The company was deploying a new router that also began to cause system disruptions at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. “The FAA’s legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” says an FAA statement. “This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds.”

Once the inconsistencies were identified, the FAA says that L3Harris blocked those two locations, and the network stabilized. However, the exact cause of the telecommunications issues are still under investigation.

Regulators are still working to identify the root cause of the issue. “The work that was done on Friday, that's been done thousands of times by L3Harris in our network,” Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said in a recent interview on ABC’s “This Week.” “It's been done thousands of times by other companies, and these issues haven't arisen, and so that's why we have to figure out what went wrong here.”

Duffy also noted that the equipment in question is several decades old: the router was originally purchased in 2001 and was also part of a system that ran on obsolete copper wiring.

Experts say that the archaic equipment underscores the urgent need to update the nation’s air traffic control system. “While the investigation continues, the incident exposed a troubling reality: America's aviation system remains vulnerable because we have relied on aging infrastructure for far too long,” says Geoff Freeman, president and CEO of US Travel Association. The “disruption was a wake-up call that Washington cannot afford to ignore.”

For many US airlines, the busy Thanksgiving travel season began with early departures on November 19 and is expected to last through December 1.

Air travel experts say that the FAA ground stop’s effects on Thanksgiving travel plans should be minimal. As of November 16, the majority of airline flight schedules were back on track. Delta was also able to restore its systems on Sunday, November 22; as of Monday, flight schedules began returning to normal but Delta fliers could still encounter lingering delays early this week.

It helps that fewer travelers are expected to fly this Thanksgiving compared to recent years. According to Mike Arnot, spokesman for Cirium, an aviation analytics company, the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is usually one of the busiest air travel days of the year. But in 2026, it’s not even slated to be in the top 50 busiest days for flying.

Travelers should still continue to check with their airline for the latest travel updates and plan to be at the airport at least two hours before takeoff for a domestic flight.

Operations are largely back on track, so many airlines have ended the flexible rebooking waivers that were issued at the beginning of the ground stop.

However, Delta is still allowing passengers who were scheduled to fly through Monday, November 16 to make changes to their flights at no extra cost through November 23. Customers' new departure dates must be on or before November 23, according to the airline’s rebooking policy.

Even if your airline no longer has a travel waiver in place, if you’re flying with a major US carrier, you likely have the ability to change your flight without paying a fee (although a difference in fare may apply). However, these policies usually do not apply to low-cost carriers or tickets booked in basic economy class.

It’s impossible to predict if a nationwide ground stop could happen again, according to Freeman of the US Travel Association. However, modernizing the air traffic control system should reduce these types of outages in the long run.

“The FAA is making progress, replacing outdated copper communications lines with high-speed fiber, upgrading radar and radio systems, and introducing technology that allows air traffic controllers to manage flights more efficiently,” Freeman says. “For travelers, these investments should mean fewer delays, more reliable flights, and greater confidence that the system can handle disruptions.”

Airline executives echoed a similar sentiment regarding the state of US air traffic control systems. “This moment must be a call to action,” United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby said in a statement emailed to media. “It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation’s Air Traffic Control system now.”

Following the ground stop, the DOT requested an additional $50.1 billion from Congress to complete its overhaul of the national air traffic control system.

#6055. Beginner’s luck: Freshmen leave it to chance at House office lottery

Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

“This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

Her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

The room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her new colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”

Not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

“Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” said Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

Rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

“I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan said.

As returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

Not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

“You’re welcome,” said Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup plan in case his number said otherwise.

“If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he said, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat currently held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

The office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

“If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira said. “This is low on my priority list.”

Some members announced their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

“Come visit me,” said Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

“First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” said Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

“We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” said Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”

Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he said of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

“These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” said Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

“Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

#6053. Storms on Both Coasts Threaten Thanksgiving Travel

Powerful storms bringing high winds and the potential for flooding could seriously disrupt commercial air travel in the U.S. during the single busiest week of the year.

Forecasters are warning that storm systems will likely strike parts of the South, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast, as well as Northern California and the Pacific Northwest. These regions are home to some of the nation’s busiest airports, through which millions of American travelers will pass this week en route to visit family and friends for Thanksgiving on Thursday.

In the Northeast, the remnants of a weakened, disorganized system were still clearing out on Monday. A much stronger storm is expected to develop in the Gulf of Mexico between Monday and Tuesday, impact parts of the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic Wednesday, and slam into the New York metro area and New England on Thanksgiving Day.

According to an advisory from the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center, strong wind gusts up to 50 mph will be felt from the Carolinas to Maine. Flooding and beach erosion could be seen in coastal areas due to the already high tides.

WPC has initiated Key Messages for a Thanksgiving Coastal Storm that is expected to impact the U.S. East Coast. pic.twitter.com/pdQuU4U4yG

Americans traveling from, through, or to these areas should prepare for the possibility of flooded roads, damage from high winds, and power outages, the agency said.

NYC Emergency Management said Sunday that the storm could bring gusts of 40 to 45 mph and about one to two inches of rain to the city.

For New York and New England, the storm will be at its strongest Thursday evening. Parts of the Adirondacks and northern New England could see ice and snow mixed in with rain.

In California, Oregon, and Washington, residents still recovering from flooding last week could be hit again by rain and strong winds. A new system is expected to move in Tuesday and Wednesday; combined with the “king tides,” the storm could cause flooding up and down the West Coast.

The impact is expected to be most severe between Portland, Oregon, and San Francisco. San Francisco’s mayor said residents should take the forecasts seriously and consider not traveling for the holiday.

The Sierra Nevada, meanwhile, will see fresh snow, meteorologists said.

Over six million people are expected to fly within the U.S. this week for Thanksgiving. The surge is already underway, with many carriers adding flights to accommodate the increased traffic. American Airlines earlier this month projected its busiest Thanksgiving week since before the COVID-19 pandemic; that prediction could hold true for other U.S. airlines as well.

AirlineGeeks will continue to monitor weather conditions and provide updates as the week progresses.

#6052. Rep. James Comer launches 2027 bid for Kentucky governor

Kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.

The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook issues, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

“If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he said.

As the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.)

Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

Known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

He made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

Comer has moved quickly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

While Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”

While Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already launched bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”

The Caribbean is a diverse region made up of over 700 islands, islets, reefs, and cays, but not all are independent countries. In total, there are 13 sovereign nations and 17 dependent territories spread across the Caribbean Sea. The independent countries include popular destinations such as Jamaica, the Bahamas, Barbados, St. Lucia, and Trinidad and Tobago. The dependent territories—like Puerto Rico (US), Martinique (France), and the Cayman Islands (UK)—offer a mix of cultural influences and governance structures. While each island varies in size, language, and history, the entire region is united by its tropical climate, vibrant cultures, and rich mix of African, European, and Indigenous heritage.

What is the best island to visit in the Caribbean?

There isn’t one “best” Caribbean island—it just depends on what kind of experience you’re seeking. Families often love Jamaica for its all-inclusive resorts, kid-friendly activities, and easy flights from the US. Surfers gravitate toward Barbados and Puerto Rico, which boast consistent swells and a laid-back surf culture. Solo travelers often choose Puerto Rico or Curaçao, thanks to their safety, walkable cities, and friendly locals. For romantic getaways, St. Lucia and Antigua are top picks—think private villas, lush rainforests, and stunning beaches perfect for couples. And for multi-generational trips, the Bahamas or Turks and Caicos stand out, offering luxury accommodations, calm beaches for kids, and plenty of excursions for all ages. Each island has its own rhythm and charm, so the “best” one depends on your travel style and interests.

When is the best time to travel to the Caribbean?

The best time to visit the Caribbean typically falls between December and April, during the region’s dry season. This period offers warm temperatures, low humidity, and minimal rainfall—ideal conditions for beach days and outdoor adventures. However, it’s also the peak tourist season, meaning higher prices and more crowds. For travelers seeking better deals and fewer tourists, the shoulder months of May, June, and November are excellent alternatives, offering good weather with occasional rain showers. The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June to November, and while severe storms are rare on most islands, it’s wise to stay informed about forecasts if traveling during this time.

Which islands in the Caribbean are the most affordable?

Jamaica and the Dominican Republic are good places to start if you're looking for budget-friendly rentals. But keep in mind that no matter which island you head to, the neighborhood and season you're traveling in matter just as much as anything else, and an exclusive beachfront address can quickly change your budget. To get the most bang for your buck, consider traveling during shoulder or off seasons, and take a look at rentals outside of the typical tourist hot spots.

Are there any islands in the Caribbean you can visit from the US without a passport?

Yes. US citizens traveling directly from the mainland can visit Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands without a passport. The US Virgin Islands include St. Thomas, St. John, and St. Croix, and travelers can also head to Puerto Rico’s offshore islands of Vieques and Culebra.

Believe it or not, Thanksgiving is around the corner. Families around the country are working on their grocery lists — and maybe keeping an eye on the wild shopping days that come after we dine with family and friends. If you're hoping to snag some great travel deals for Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday, TPG has a dedicated page where you can find our favorite deals.

And if you need a little inspiration for your next vacation, we just released our annual Where to Go list for 2027. This year's list ranges from Texas Hill Country to Tunisia and from the Cayman Islands to Kazakhstan.

Now, here's the hotel news you need to know about from this week.

Hyatt is expanding its lifestyle footprint with the opening of the first Andaz in Australia. The Andaz Gold Coast, located in sunny Queensland, will have 202 rooms and plans to "redefine coastal luxury through a distinctive blend of expressive Australian design and immersive experiences inspired by the people, places, and creative spirit of the Gold Coast," according to a statement from Hyatt. The property is near the beaches of Broadbeach, and features a series of bars and restaurants, plus a lively pool club offering live music and community-focused barbecues.

Also in Queensland, Brisbane will welcome a Park Hyatt in 2031, ahead of the 2032 Brisbane Olympics. Brisbane is one of my favorite cities, so I can't wait (though I'll have to) for the 201-room property not far from Suncorp Stadium, which will host a series of soccer and rugby events. Many details about the property are still under wraps, but if it's even half as great as the Park Hyatt Sydney, we know it'll be a great hotel.

If you haven't had the chance to visit Houston, I can't recommend it enough. The city is home to diverse cultures, incredible food and the Houston Livestock Show and Rodeo, one of the biggest rodeos in the world. If you find yourself in Beyoncé's hometown, consider a stay at the JW Marriott Houston Downtown, which just completed a years-long head-to-toe remodel. The hotel now features fresh rooms, including 56 new rooms, a redesigned lobby restaurant and a total revamp of the hotel's food and beverage offerings.

Monti, my favorite neighborhood in Rome, feels like stepping back in time. Or, at least into a movie set, thanks to its beautiful vine-covered walls, cobblestone streets and lively energy near the Colosseum. In 2028, it'll also be home to Hortus Monti Rome, part of Hilton's upscale LXR Hotels & Resorts. The hotel is spread across six historic Umbertine-era buildings, according to a statement from Hilton and features a central garden, a spa, bars and restaurants and more.

Until then, Hilton fans should check into Rome Cavalieri, one of the most popular Waldorf Astoria hotels in the world.

The Coke versus Pepsi debate is a serious one, and people tend to have strong opinions about which is better. While I'm a Diet Dr. Pepper fanatic myself, it looks like Hyatt is doubling down on its relationship with Pepsi. The company just renewed its contract, making PepsiCo the preferred beverage partner across 700 Hyatt properties in the United States. The agreement also extends to certain PepsiCo snack products.

Earlier this year, Marriott ousted Pepsi and made Coca-Cola its "global beverage partner across several categories, including carbonated soft drinks and a growing range of hydration and functional beverages."

#6048. What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”

In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

Black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They showed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

The number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

"I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson plan?

Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

Scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she said.

Colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”

Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

Mary C. Curtis has worked at The New York Times, The Baltimore Sun, The Charlotte Observer, as national correspondent for Politics Daily, and is a senior facilitator with The OpEd Project. She is host of the CQ Roll Call “Equal Time with Mary C. Curtis” podcast. Follow her on X @mcurtisnc3.

#6044. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

#6041. These incoming members of Congress have been here before

Rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

“I said, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

Unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”

Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

A couple years ago, Killin was working as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff. But she started out on the Hill.

“It is helpful to know, as I joke, where the bathrooms are, but I still feel like I have a lot to learn,” said the Army veteran, who unseated Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a Colorado Springs-area district.

She served as the top staffer for three House Democrats: Donna Shalala of Florida, Carolyn Maloney of New York and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.

“I’ve actually opened up two freshman offices, so it’s helpful to have done that before,” Killin said.

White will be just the third person in modern times to hold the job of nonvoting D.C. delegate. He replaces retiring Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton — also his former boss.

Before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

“I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

One of just a few Republican women in the freshman class, Gruters said she “never in a million years” imagined coming to Congress herself, despite her years as a staffer.

She will replace retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan in Florida’s 16th District, after once serving as his operations director. She also worked as district director for Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla.

“I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Gruters, whose husband leads the Republican National Committee.

Rogers added another title to his résumé last week: freshman class president.

His fellow incoming Republicans tapped him for the role. Not so long ago, he was working for the Senate Judiciary Committee, fresh off a stint at the white-shoe law firm White & Case.

In 2025 he served as general counsel for Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are currently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers said, describing it as “deplorable.”

Rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

García’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”

The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech company Oracle.

He also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

“I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State New York.

Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

Villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.

A decade ago, he was an intern for Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif. And the progressive also interned for former California state Rep. Rudy Salas, who made unsuccessful bids to unseat Valadao in 2022 and 2024.

A San Diego City councilmember, Von Wilpert flipped the seat held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who decided not to run for reelection under a map redrawn by Democrats.

When she worked for the National Labor Relations Board in 2016, she was detailed to the House Education and Labor Committee, working under ranking member Robert C. Scott, D-Va.

Jackie Wang and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

A previous version of this report misstated when Rudy Salas ran for office.

#6040. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister currently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

In a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he said when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he said, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

#6038. How Airbus Fixed The A350's Cracking Problem Without A Fleet-Wide Grounding

Aircraft development has its ups and downs, especially when it comes to advancing aircraft design. When reports first surfaced regarding localized surface degradation on the Airbus A350, it sparked an intense public and legal debate over the long-term airworthiness of composite commercial transport aircraft. This guide explores how the European airframe manufacturer resolved this sophisticated surface tension issue through targeted material adjustments, without incurring the massive operational and financial disruptions of a fleet-wide grounding.

Unlike traditional aluminum commercial aircraft, modern twin-aisle jets rely heavily on carbon fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) to reduce structural weight and optimize fuel efficiency on ultra-long-haul routes. However, introducing these advanced non-metallic materials introduces entirely new operational variables for exterior coatings and lightning-protection layers.

The cause of the surface cracking issue on the widebody comes down to a complex material science phenomenon involving highly dissimilar structural layers. Carbon fiber reinforced plastic behaves very differently from traditional aerospace aluminum when exposed to the extreme environmental fluctuations of international flight profiles. Specifically, it has a remarkably low coefficient of thermal expansion, meaning the composite fuselage shell barely changes its physical dimensions whether it is sitting on a hot tarmac or cruising at high altitudes.

The exterior coatings applied to the aircraft, along with the underlying expanded copper foil layer used for lightning strike protection, exhibit markedly different expansion and contraction characteristics. When an aircraft departs an equatorial runway at 110 degrees Fahrenheit (43.3 degrees Celsius) and climbs rapidly to a cruise altitude where ambient temperatures plummet to minus 65 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 53.9 degrees Celsius), the swift temperature drop creates immense mechanical stress at the interface layer. What happens is that the outer paint and metallic foil attempt to shrink while the underlying composite shell remains completely rigid, so the resulting shear forces stretch the exterior coating beyond its physical limits.

This structural tension caused the outermost layers of paint to develop fine cracks, flakes, and localized blisters, primarily along the manufacturing joints where different fuselage panels meet. These surface blemishes were visually apparent to passengers and airline maintenance teams; however, deep non-destructive testing confirmed the peeling was entirely restricted to the superficial exterior layers and the thin protective foil mesh. The underlying structural carbon-fiber fuselage frame remained completely intact, dry, and unaffected by the separation of the exterior coating.

Despite aggressive demands for an immediate worldwide grounding of the fleet from Qatar Airways, international aviation oversight bodies maintained a highly measured, data-driven approach. EASA and the FAA launched exhaustive technical reviews of the airframe manufacturing data rather than resorting to precautionary operational bans. Safety regulators need clear evidence of a structural or systemic flight safety hazard before taking the drastic step of halting a global aircraft fleet.

The technical analysis quickly demonstrated that the paint degradation did not compromise the underlying structural airworthiness of the twinjet. Regulatory directives mandated localized inspections of the lightning protection mesh on specific early-production airframes rather than pulling the type from active service. Doing so allowed the vast majority of international operators to maintain their scheduled passenger networks while also firmly addressing cosmetic paint issues during normal hangar visits.

Qatar Airways chose to unilaterally withdraw more than 20 of its jets from service over the cosmetic dispute, but even still, global safety authorities repeatedly verified that the multi-layered composite hull remained completely safe for continuous transoceanic operations. Regardless, the airline remained opposed to these views, and launched a legal battle in response.

Airbus started its own legal action against Qatar Airways in a UK court on Monday, asking a judge for $220 million over two undelivered A350s.

To completely eliminate the interface stresses that drive cosmetic issues, design teams had to re-engineer the conductive lightning strike protection layer embedded directly beneath the paint coat. The original manufacturing layout used expanded copper foil mesh, a material produced by stretching a solid sheet of copper to form an open diamond pattern. It is highly effective at conducting electrical currents, but the properties of this expanded mesh resist the subtle micro-movements of the surrounding composite skin, acting as a rigid barrier that concentrated shear forces directly into the paint layers.

Airbus resolved this structural mismatch by developing an inline material substitution, replacing the traditional expanded mesh with an advanced perforated copper foil (PCF). This new foil variant features precisely drilled, uniform microscopic apertures that give the metallic layer significantly greater multi-directional flexibility. So, by allowing the metallic lightning shield to flex in perfect harmony with both the underlying carbon fiber skin and the outer paint primers, the perforated design eliminates localized shear stresses that caused the original coatings to fracture.

The upgraded material standard began rolling out to active assembly lines in late 2022, so newer production airframes left the factory with built-in protection against premature coating separation. Airbus's quick evolution highlights how aerospace manufacturing teams can deploy an engineering improvement to protect long-term fleet reliability without halting active factory production lines. The implementation of the perforated foil standard permanently corrected the root material conflict, keeping widebody deliveries free from early paint degradation.

For the hundreds of aircraft already operating within global airline networks, the engineering fix took the form of a localized repair methodology that could be executed during standard maintenance cycles. The issue, however, is that stripping and repainting the entire exterior of a widebody requires weeks of hangar time and costs millions of dollars per airframe. To protect the integrity of airline scheduling, technical teams developed a targeted microlayer patch protocol that focuses exclusively on the affected panel joints.

Maintenance crews follow a highly precise procedure: first, they sand down the localized areas of degraded paint, carefully clean the underlying metallic foil shield, and then apply a specialized microlayer resin patch compound. The advanced composite resin restores the smooth aerodynamic profile of the fuselage section while reinforcing the physical bond between the composite skin and the surrounding lightning protection layer. These targeted touch-ups require only a few days of downtime, allowing airlines to seamlessly complete the work during routine intermediate service stops.

Operators like Delta Air Lines, Singapore Airlines, and Lufthansawere able to maintain complete network integrity throughout the cosmetic crisis, managing the paint blemishes through data-driven line maintenance rather than emotional operational halts. These carriers avoided massive scheduling disruptions for passengers, successfully mitigating complex material issues without harming corporate profitability or fleet utilization rates.

Even as these carriers worked to return to normal operations, there was, of course, Qatar Airways, with its paint-degradation dispute centered on whether the fine surface cracking compromised the aircraft's lightning-strike protection system, particularly around the high-capacity fuel tanks embedded within the wings. Commercial passenger aircraft are struck by lightning an average of once per year, according to Airbus, and so the structural integrity of the conductive exterior skin is vital for protecting sensitive onboard systems. Any compromise to this system near fuel storage zones would immediately elevate the issue to a severe airworthiness hazard.

Detailed engineering documentation and teardown inspections demonstrated that the widebody wing skin incorporates multiple redundant layers of protection. Even in localized areas where the outermost paint layers showed visible cosmetic cracking, the continuous path for safe electrical dissipation remained fully functional. Testing verified that the underlying metallic mesh retained its full capability to conduct large electrical currents and safely route them across the exterior skin to the static wicks, keeping the energy well away from internal fuel vapor barriers.

Regulatory investigations confirmed that the superficial cracking did not create localized electrical hot spots or spark hazards near the wing structures. This technical validation provided the scientific justification needed for safety authorities to reject any mandatory grounding orders and gave operators the complete engineering confidence required to keep their widebody fleets flying safely while factory teams prepared the permanent production material updates.

The resolution of the surface cracking issue ultimately finalized a long-term step forward in how composite widebodies are manufactured, finished, and managed at the factory level. Now, by incorporating the perforated copper foil standard and updated paint-curing processes directly into the central assembly infrastructure in Toulouse, new A350 aircraft are already protected against a recurrence of this issue.

Now we can look back on this multi-year aerospace saga as the validation of advanced composite materials under intense real-world operational and environmental scrutiny. The ability to isolate, analyze, and correct an unprecedented material-interface problem without disrupting global fleet operations demonstrates just how far modern commercial aerospace engineering has come. It demonstrates that complex material science challenges can be resolved through precise technical iterations rather than sweeping operational stoppages.

The global fleet continues to accumulate millions of flight hours across demanding intercontinental flight paths, bringing this crucial learning curve in the industry-wide transition away from traditional aluminum airframes with it. The engineering adjustments developed during this period ensure that the twin-engine widebody platforms are an exceptionally efficient, long-term asset capable of leading the world's premier route networks. Empirical science has saved the A350 today with a more resilient material standard that secures the operational future of the aircraft.

#6037. Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

There’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

“There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

“There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”

“I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

“We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet announced — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin said.

#6036. Lufthansa Management Threatens To Massively Shrink Airline, Lay Off Employees

Lufthansa is the “flagship” airline of Lufthansa Group, yet somehow, is the least profitable airline in the whole organization. 2026 was supposed to be an exciting turnaround year for Lufthansa, as it’s even the carrier’s 100th anniversary.

Unfortunately things haven’t turned out so great. Earlier this year, the carrier dealt with massive labor issues, and back-to-back-to-back strikes. Just a few months ago, the company’s senior management claimed it wanted to turn over a new leaf with labor relations, and stop fighting with employees, so that it could find long term solutions.

How is that working out? Well, Lufthansa pilots are just days from possibly being able to strike again, no agreement has been reached for long term peace with employees, and management is threatening to massively shrink its mainline operation. In other words, it’s just another day at Lufthansa!

Lufthansa and its pilots have been in negotiations for quite some time over the future of the company. As you’d expect, broadly speaking, negotiations revolve around pay and future flying opportunities. As you’d expect at any airline, employees want as much flying as possible, and as big of a fleet as possible, since that’s what maximizes their compensation.

The issue with Lufthansa Group management is that the company’s solution to everything is to simply create new, low cost subsidiaries. And if Lufthansa Group management doesn’t like the terms with its subsidiaries, then it just shuts down the subsidiaries and creates new ones.

So that brings us to the current issue. Essentially, Lufthansa’s problem is that the airline doesn’t make money on short haul flights, given high costs and intense competition. So we’ve seen the carrier increasingly outsourcing this flying to Lufthansa City Airlines, a subsidiary with lower operating costs, operating the same kinds of planes as you’ll see in the mainline fleet.

Lufthansa is asking its pilots to accept wage freezes, and is promising a certain level of career development opportunities. Pilots aren’t happy with what’s being proposed, so what’s Lufthansa’s solution?

Management is reportedly proposing a new plan to the supervisory board, which would see the core Lufthansa brand massively reduce its regional flying, and largely outsource this to lower cost operations, like Lufthansa City Airlines. The idea would be to make Lufthansa primarily a long haul airline, and then have much of the short haul flying be operated by a subsidiary.

Lufthansa’s mainline fleet currently consists of 260+ planes, with another 120+ planes on order. One proposal would see the mainline fleet reduced to 100 long haul aircraft and 100 short haul aircraft, with other planes being assigned to Lufthansa City Airlines.

One radical proposal could even see Lufthansa exclusively have a long haul fleet and ditch short haul flying, though it’s noted that this isn’t the most likely scenario, and it could take several years for something like that to be implemented.

Keep in mind that going back to 2017, Lufthansa had guaranteed pilots a minimum fleet size of 325 aircraft, but it terminated that agreement at the end of 2021. So it’s really hard for employees to trust any promises by management, when they can just be terminated.

There’s no denying that labor relations can be incredibly challenging, and that the economics of intra-Europe flying are also tough, when you have competitors like Ryanair, though Lufthansa doesn’t face nearly as much competition on that front as other carriers. Then again, Frankfurt (FRA) and Munich (MUC) aren’t exactly massively leisure destinations either.

Most airline employees want their company to succeed, and just want to be compensated fairly. Admittedly economics don’t always align. But what I find incredibly toxic is the approach taken by Lufthansa management. Let’s compare it to a marriage (which I think is a fair way to view the relationship between management and employees, since they’re “stuck” with one another).

Lufthansa’s approach is to constantly threaten employees by saying that “if you don’t do what we want, we’ll just get rid of you.” That’s simply not a good faith way to approach things. Why would Lufthansa employees trust management, when they’ve repeatedly torn up contracts, and shown employees they simply don’t care? It would be like threatening to leave your spouse every time you have an issue, rather than trying to find a solution.

Nothing against Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr personally, but I don’t understand how the board thinks he’s the best person for the job. Where’s the accountability for the endless management mistakes that have horribly impacted Lufthansa’s bottom line? Lufthansa’s employees are paying the price for the lack of success that comes as a result of all of Lufthansa’s errors, from the botched Allegris rollout, to Lufthansa’s very bad luck with new aircraft orders.

And before anyone says “oh, but the unions,” contrast what has happened at Lufthansa Group to what has happened at Air France-KLM, under the leadership of Ben Smith. Smith has now been CEO at Air France for over eight years, and there hasn’t been a single strike under his leadership. Under the previous Air France-KLM CEO, there were endless strikes, and the situation got so bad that senior executives were being chased up a fence and having their clothes ripped off.

This shows that good labor relations absolutely can happen, balancing the needs of employees and the company. But it requires showing employees that you actually care about the company and their future. What was one of Smith’s first orders of business when he took the job at Air France-KLM? He eliminated Joon, the low cost carrier at the airline that was supposed to basically be a labor arbitrage opportunity. That was a way to show employees how much he respected them, and that he wanted a fair agreement, rather than one that would undermine them.

Meanwhile Spohr’s solution to literally everything is to just threaten to start new subsidiaries or shut down existing subsidiaries. The irony is that Spohr started his career as a pilot, so you’d think he’d have respect for employees, having been on the other side. But clearly once he became senior management, his love for aviation turned into disdain for employees.

A few months ago, Lufthansa management claimed it wanted to turn over a new leaf when it comes to labor relations. That didn’t last long, because now the airline is back to its “do what we say or we’ll create a new subsidiary” approach.

I don’t have a strong opinion on the exact negotiations as such. Obviously it’s a tough time for aviation, and intra-Europe flying is challenging. But if you ask me, the toxicity that has been created by Lufthansa management due to the lack of good faith negotiations just can’t be undone.

If your only solution to everything is “oh, we’ll create a new subsidiary,” and if that doesn’t work, maybe it’s time for a new strategy. The fact that American CEO Robert Isom and Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr still have their jobs are two of the industry’s greatest mysteries.

What do you make of Lufthansa’s latest threat to employees?
