#5970. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

There's a hidden menace out there. Big-money projects built at the behest of the oligarchy are taking huge amounts of water from our communities,...

When aging telecommunications routers overloaded and forced the Federal Aviation Administration to issue a sudden nationwide ground stop, thousands of flights were frozen across the country. For the millions of travelers stranded in terminals, and for the air traffic controllers forced to manage congested skies with equipment built over two decades ago, the crisis was no surprise. It was the predictable result of a political system where lawmakers routinely put local earmarks and self-interest ahead of public safety.

​Across major hubs from Newark and Chicago to Atlanta, the invisible digital backbone keeping aircraft separated is running on borrowed time. Legacy copper wiring, analog voice switches, and obsolete radar systems need a complete, $50 billion overhaul. It is not just internal aviation officials sounding the alarm. Independent aviation experts, safety boards, and aerospace engineering coalitions have repeatedly cautioned that the nation’s air traffic control network is operating on a dangerous margin of error. Yet even as these warnings mount, the money required to fix the system remains trapped behind a wall of congressional gridlock.

Rove is offering 1,500 free miles just for signing up. You don’t have to book a trip, buy anything, or complete any other transaction. I specifically asked about an activity requirement, and Rove confirmed that new members get the miles instantly. I’ve written quite a bit about Rove, and asked them to improve the offer available through my link. This is three times the standard 500-mile referral signup bonus. Just like normal referrals, I receive Rove Miles when someone signs up through this link. It doesn’t cost you anything. In fact it gets you much more than not using this link. They’ve also created a hotel booking code for readers: 1,500 miles for joining: Use this link to create your new account. There’s no purchase requirement. 5,000 additional miles on your first hotel booking of $500 or more: Enter promo code VFTW when booking through Rove. A new member who uses both offers would earn 6,500 bonus miles, on top of the normal miles from their qualifying hotel booking. You can also just take the signup miles. And 5,000 miles on a $500 booking is twice what Rove offered at that spending level during its May promotion. What You Can Do With These Miles Rove is a free rewards program that lets you earn miles from hotel and flight bookings, online shopping, dining and gift cards. You don’t have to apply for a credit card, and you can earn rewards from the card you use to pay as well. Their transfer partners include familiar programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France KLM Flying Blue, Qatar Airways Privilege Club and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. They also have programs that are harder to access through the major bank currencies, including Lufthansa Miles & More (for better availability of business and first class awards), Japan Airlines Mileage Bank (better availability of awards, lower prices on partner awards), Air India Maharaja Club (United awards starting at just 3,500 points) and Copa ConnectMiles (Emirates awards with no fuel surcharges). Rove has a 2,000-mile minimum for partner transfers. You don’t need a hotel stay to earn additional miles. I’ve covered Rove’s dining program and instant gift card rewards, and just wrote about its personalized shopping offers of up to 25 miles per dollar. When The Hotel Bonus Makes Sense You can also redeem Rove Miles directly for travel. As I wrote last month, I can usually get around 1.5 cents apiece redeeming them for hotel stays that still earn hotel points and elite status credit. Using that benchmark, the 5,000-mile hotel bonus is worth about $75 toward travel. On a qualifying $500 booking, that’s an extra 15% in value before the booking’s regular rewards. Expressed another way, the promo adds 10 miles per dollar at exactly $500 in qualifying spend. I’ve been particularly interested in Rove’s Loyalty Eligible hotel rates. There are two different kinds of bookings to compare: Loyalty Eligible rates generally earn 5 Rove miles per dollar, while preserving eligibility for the hotel’s own points, elite night credit and status benefits. The hotel charges your card, which can make paying with that chain’s credit card attractive. Rove Rates can offer more Rove miles, with the site advertising up to 25 per dollar, but generally give up the hotel loyalty program earnings and benefits. That tradeoff is easier at an independent hotel where you wouldn’t earn chain points anyway. I’d take the free signup miles. For the hotel offer, enter VFTW and consider the rate you’re selecting before booking for the 5,000-mile bonus. As I wrote last month, I can usually get around 1.5 cents apiece redeeming them for hotel stays that still earn hotel points and elite status credit. Using that benchmark, the 5,000-mile hotel bonus is worth about $75 toward travel. On a qualifying $500 booking, that’s an extra 15% in value before the booking’s regular rewards. Expressed another way, the promo adds 10 miles per dollar at exactly $500 in qualifying spend. I’ve been particularly interested in Rove’s Loyalty Eligible hotel rates. There are two different kinds of bookings to compare: Loyalty Eligible rates generally earn 5 Rove miles per dollar, while preserving eligibility for the hotel’s own points, elite night credit and status benefits. The hotel charges your card, which can make paying with that chain’s credit card attractive. Rove Rates can offer more Rove miles, with the site advertising up to 25 per dollar, but generally give up the hotel loyalty program earnings and benefits. That tradeoff is easier at an independent hotel where you wouldn’t earn chain points anyway. I’d take the free signup miles. For the hotel offer, enter VFTW and consider the rate you’re selecting before booking for the 5,000-mile bonus. Rove is a free rewards program that lets you earn miles from hotel and flight bookings, online shopping, dining and gift cards. You don’t have to apply for a credit card, and you can earn rewards from the card you use to pay as well.

Their transfer partners include familiar programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France KLM Flying Blue, Qatar Airways Privilege Club and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

They also have programs that are harder to access through the major bank currencies, including Lufthansa Miles & More (for better availability of business and first class awards), Japan Airlines Mileage Bank (better availability of awards, lower prices on partner awards), Air India Maharaja Club (United awards starting at just 3,500 points) and Copa ConnectMiles (Emirates awards with no fuel surcharges). Rove has a 2,000-mile minimum for partner transfers.

You don’t need a hotel stay to earn additional miles. I’ve covered Rove’s dining program and instant gift card rewards, and just wrote about its personalized shopping offers of up to 25 miles per dollar.

Why is it asking for my checking account information? That’s a non-starter for me. I’ll link a credit card but not my checking account.

Actually, I still got the points even though I terminated the process when it asked for my checking account to be linked.

Lol they give you 1,500 miles, but the minimum transfer out is 2,000 miles

@beachfan Barry’s right, the miles post before you link anything, so you can just skip the bank step. The 5,000 on a first $500 hotel booking is the juicier part, as long as the rate isn’t padded. FWIW you can look up Arbitrica or similar free tools that check the same hotel from a ton of countries to find kind of the lowest price in the world, since rates and inventory vary by country. If their price is close, take the miles

#5967. Rove Launches Elite Status With Third Night Free Hotel Awards—Will This Turn Deal Chasers Into Loyal Customers?

Rove is launching elite status with a third night free on eligible hotel awards, and top tier Diamond members get two free nights on a six night stay. You can qualify through travel bookings, shopping and dining, without holding a particular credit card. The benefits can make Rove more rewarding. They may also bean attempt to address the problem I’ve had with the business from the beginning: when you attract customers by giving them the best deal, what keeps them around when somebody else offers more? How Rove’s New Status Program Works Rove Status launches November 23, 2026. Everyone starts as a Member, and there are three earned tiers. You need both qualifying miles and qualifying transactions during a calendar year: Status Qualifying Miles Qualifying Transactions Gold 50,000 5 Platinum 125,000 10 Diamond 250,000 20 Qualifying activity from earlier in 2026 counts retroactively, and status earned in 2026 lasts through December 31, 2027. Rove clarified what counts: Transaction earnings count, including elevated rates and status bonuses. Miles associated with paid travel bookings, shopping, gift cards and dining qualify. That includes purchased Miles Boost earnings. Flat bonuses don’t count. An offer of 2,500 bonus miles for spending $500 won’t add those 2,500 miles to your status progress, although the qualifying purchase and its ordinary earnings still count. Referrals, transfers, customer support credits and other miles unrelated to a cash transaction don’t count. Pure award redemptions don’t earn qualifying miles or transactions either. Rove makes an exception for miles + cash bookings. Shopping, dining and gift cards count based on the purchase date. Travel counts when it’s completed: hotel checkout or the last flight of a multi-segment trip. Booking a hotel in December for a January checkout won’t help with 2026 status. Late posting doesn’t move activity into the wrong year. If a December purchase posts in January, it still counts toward 2026 qualification, and Rove can award the resulting status after the new year begins. The spending required depends on how quickly you earn qualifying miles. At an average of 10 qualifying miles per dollar, Gold takes $5,000, Platinum $12,500, and Diamond $25,000. At 25 qualifying miles per dollar, Diamond takes $10,000. At 5, it takes $50,000. You still need the required number of qualifying transactions. And once you earn status, the extra miles from eligible elite earning bonuses help you reach the next tier or requalify. Here are the announced benefits: Benefit Gold Platinum Diamond Free night on eligible Rove Rate awards Fifth night Fourth night Third night Discount on eligible paid hotel rates, excluding Loyalty Eligible 5% 8% 10% Additional shopping miles per dollar at select brands Up to 5 Up to 8 Up to 10 Paid Miles Boost limit Up to 12x Up to 15x Up to 20x Rove’s partner transfer minimum 1,500 miles 1,000 miles No minimum Extra transfer bonus during eligible promotions None listed 10 percentage points 15 percentage points Customer support Gold priority Platinum priority Diamond priority and Diamond Desk All three earned tiers also offer parental leave: new parents can extend their status expiration by 12 months. Rove says additional partner benefits are coming. The Free Hotel Night Is The Biggest Benefit — With An Important Limitation A third night free can be substantial, and Rove confirms a six night Diamond stay receives two free nights. The deduction uses the average nightly price, so a cheaper third night doesn’t shrink the benefit. On a three or six night Diamond award, the eligible award cost falls by a third. Platinum saves 25% on a four night award and Gold saves 20% on a five night award. Rove says the free night calculation excludes only fees due at the hotel, such as resort fees or locally collected taxes. (Those charges remain payable.) That also makes each mile worth more. A third off the miles required means 50% more value per mile. And I generally get about 1.5 cents per Rove Mile as it is. But both the free award nights and the paid hotel discounts exclude Loyalty Eligible bookings. Those have been my favorite use of Rove miles. The free nights apply to Rove Rate awards, which are going to be third party bookings (may not earn points, status credit or receive status benefits). With Loyalty Eligible stays, you can redeem Rove miles and still earn hotel points and elite night credit, while receiving your hotel status benefits. Rove Rate bookings don’t earn those hotel points or nights, and don’t guarantee your hotel elite benefits. I’d be most interested in the free night benefit at independent hotels, or on stays where I don’t have valuable hotel status to give up. A discounted three or six night award could be a much better use of miles than the same stay was before. Rove explains that it can’t offer the paid hotel discount on Loyalty Eligible rates because the hotel is the merchant of record and Rove doesn’t control the pricing. I’d note that commissions are lower, too, so it would also be costlier to offer. Extra Transfer Bonuses And Shopping Bonuses The extra transfer bonuses apply on top of eligible existing promotions, and Rove confirms they’re additive. A 40% promotion becomes 50% for Platinum and 55% for Diamond. At a partner with a normal 1:1 ratio, transferring 10,000 Rove miles during that offer would yield 14,000 partner miles ordinarily, 15,000 for Platinum, or 15,500 for Diamond. There’s no standing 15% Diamond bonus on every transfer. The shopping bonuses mean additional miles per dollar. Diamond’s maximum is 10 extra miles per dollar at select brands, rather than multiplying the ordinary earning rate by ten. These bonuses aren’t available on everything you buy, but where offered they improve both your redeemable points-earn and status progress. Lower transfer minimums are useful for topping off an airline account. Rove’s ordinary minimum is 2,000 miles, though individual partners can have their own minimums or increments. Removing Rove’s minimum is a nice convenience. Rove Needs Customers Who Come Back I’ve written about Rove’s customer challenge. An airline starts with passengers who need its flights. A hotel company starts with guests who need rooms in its locations. Rove has to persuade people to use its platform for purchases they were already making. They’ve done that by frequently being more rewarding than competitors. That’s attracted attention and business, but it also attracts the loyalty equivalent of hot money. Customers compare offers, take the richest one, and potentially. Status gives the next transaction value beyond the miles it earns immediately. Someone approaching Gold might choose Rove even when another portal offers a little more. Someone who already has Diamond may keep earning because they want enough miles for another discounted three night stay. And even without doing the math, people like reaching a tier and dislike losing it. The transaction requirements push customers beyond one big purchase. Rove’s expansion into dining, shopping and an app gives customers more reasons to return between trips. Status gives those activities a common target. And while a rich acquisition offer pays someone who might never come back, a status discount generally requires another booking before Rove incurs the cost. Some members won’t use it. Rove can direct more of its rewards spending toward customers who return, instead of having to offer the biggest public bonus to everyone. The hotel award benefit also encourages members to redeem within Rove instead of transferring their miles to an airline. That may be cheaper where Rove has favorable hotel inventory costs. I’d Like To See More Than Bigger Rebates What’s largely missing is the experience of being treated differently. An airline can give you a better seat that would otherwise go empty. A hotel can upgrade you to an unsold suite. The customer may value that far more than it costs to deliver. Rove doesn’t control those seats and rooms, so promising similar treatment would require agreements with partners. Rove is giving better customer service with status – I asked what the Diamond Desk actually does, and they shared it provides maximum customer support priority and a dedicated email address. Rove is doing the rewarding part well, but they haven’t quite yet figured out recognition which is just as much a part of loyalty. Rove is doing the rewarding part well, but they haven’t quite yet figured out recognition which is just as much a part of loyalty. Topics on this pageCustomer loyalty improvement recommender system (clirs)Frequent-flyer programLoyalty programMileTravel agency+2 more More From View from the Wing

The extra transfer bonuses apply on top of eligible existing promotions, and Rove confirms they’re additive. A 40% promotion becomes 50% for Platinum and 55% for Diamond. At a partner with a normal 1:1 ratio, transferring 10,000 Rove miles during that offer would yield 14,000 partner miles ordinarily, 15,000 for Platinum, or 15,500 for Diamond. There’s no standing 15% Diamond bonus on every transfer.

The shopping bonuses mean additional miles per dollar. Diamond’s maximum is 10 extra miles per dollar at select brands, rather than multiplying the ordinary earning rate by ten. These bonuses aren’t available on everything you buy, but where offered they improve both your redeemable points-earn and status progress.

Lower transfer minimums are useful for topping off an airline account. Rove’s ordinary minimum is 2,000 miles, though individual partners can have their own minimums or increments. Removing Rove’s minimum is a nice convenience.

I’ve written about Rove’s customer challenge. An airline starts with passengers who need its flights. A hotel company starts with guests who need rooms in its locations. Rove has to persuade people to use its platform for purchases they were already making. They’ve done that by frequently being more rewarding than competitors. That’s attracted attention and business, but it also attracts the loyalty equivalent of hot money. Customers compare offers, take the richest one, and potentially. Status gives the next transaction value beyond the miles it earns immediately. Someone approaching Gold might choose Rove even when another portal offers a little more. Someone who already has Diamond may keep earning because they want enough miles for another discounted three night stay. And even without doing the math, people like reaching a tier and dislike losing it. The transaction requirements push customers beyond one big purchase. Rove’s expansion into dining, shopping and an app gives customers more reasons to return between trips. Status gives those activities a common target. And while a rich acquisition offer pays someone who might never come back, a status discount generally requires another booking before Rove incurs the cost. Some members won’t use it. Rove can direct more of its rewards spending toward customers who return, instead of having to offer the biggest public bonus to everyone. The hotel award benefit also encourages members to redeem within Rove instead of transferring their miles to an airline. That may be cheaper where Rove has favorable hotel inventory costs. I’d Like To See More Than Bigger Rebates What’s largely missing is the experience of being treated differently. An airline can give you a better seat that would otherwise go empty. A hotel can upgrade you to an unsold suite. The customer may value that far more than it costs to deliver. Rove doesn’t control those seats and rooms, so promising similar treatment would require agreements with partners. Rove is giving better customer service with status – I asked what the Diamond Desk actually does, and they shared it provides maximum customer support priority and a dedicated email address. Rove is doing the rewarding part well, but they haven’t quite yet figured out recognition which is just as much a part of loyalty. You continue to highlight what I’ll call the Citi Strata Elite problem. I like Rove. It’s a nice program. There’s real value there. But there’s no pot of gold at the end of the rainbow in terms of making my travel experience easier (airline status / more than 4 lounge passes). So it’s hard to get too excited about the program in general, even though it potentially offers some really good value. Versus, say, AA Hotels where I can get 12x automatically on the spend plus offers that get me tons additional miles/LP towards status.

The number of transactions is a bit meaningless when you can buy $5 gift cards. But the spend requirement is real here – if you are assuming an average of 20x miles from your Rove spend (which could be high but who knows) that’s $12.5k in spend to get top status. If you are regularly staying places three nights or longer, could be a valuable benefit as well.

But would I rather have free access to MCE/extra legroom seating versus using a hotel free night stay benefit a few times a year? Probably! But that’s just me, based on my travel patterns. YMMV.

I’ve been using Rove but also finding a lot of issues. – Almost always, the offer they show me “no longer availabe” when I go to check out and a new offer is shown instead. – There are pricing games going on, where for examples, taxes change dramatically if you and or remove breakfast or whether it’s refundable. (The taxes in this case are not related to the difference in cost.) – I was booking something the other day and they kept declining the transactions. But Chase swears they didn’t get those transactions. – And what I consider the worst thing, the photos and descriptions they have on rooms often does not match what you actually get. They tend to put the same photos on multiple room types, so if you don’t know this and don’t verify on other sites you get screwed. – I find there overall presentation of hotels terrible too, so you basically have to find what you want elsewhere and search here just for price. It’s definitely not a one stop shop. So overall, I’m still not sure it’s worth it.

#5966. Caring for Aging Loved Ones Is Not an Injustice

SNL’s ‘Sister’ skit has ignited a national discussion about caregiving, but are we taking the right lessons from it?

John Mulaney appears in Saturday Night Live’s “Sister” sketch

Saturday Night Live struck a nerve with its recent “Sister” skit, a spoof advertisement for a supposedly revolutionary elder-care service that is free, available around the clock, and conveniently happens to be your sister. The skit is funny because it captures something many families recognize: When an aging parent needs help, it’s often the women who step up, while male relatives carry on with their lives largely uninterrupted.

There’s certainly some truth to this, but there’s a difference between objecting to an unfair division of caregiving responsibilities and treating those responsibilities as inherently oppressive. The suggestion that our elder-care challenges are largely a product of sexism, or that women who take on these responsibilities have simply been conditioned to accept their own exploitation, misses the bigger issue. This interpretation not only diminishes the contributions of female caregivers but also feeds into a troubling cultural narrative: that caring for the people we love is an injustice rather than a responsibility inherent to family.

Heather Madden is the vice president for policy initiatives at Independent Women.

On “Caring for Aging Loved Ones Is Not an Injustice”

#5965. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

#5964. American Airlines Will Displace Philadelphia Pilots—Blames Union For Rejecting A321XLR Staffing Deal

American Airlines says a “significant number” of Philadelphia pilots will be displaced from their current positions after their union’s board rejected a deal on staffing Airbus A321XLR flights to Europe. The airline is reopening a domestic Airbus pilot base and shrinking its international one for June 2027. That can change which trips pilots fly, the schedules they can hold, and potentially their commutes. American is blaming the union for rejecting what it calls an “objectively better path forward.” Aviation watchdog JonNYC shares the company’s message to pilots: When we publish our June 2027 vacancy announcement tomorrow, you will see that we are reopening a PHL A320 Domestic base (Section 17.S.1) and reducing the PHL A320 International base. This will, unfortunately, result in the displacement of a significant number of pilots from the PHL A320 International base (Section 17.D). The airline says it had agreed to a term sheet with the Allied Pilots Association, completed the contractual language, and expected a signed side agreement. The union’s board rejected it November 6. November 22, 2026 The dispute connects two things that don’t seem related at first blush: which pilots get lucrative extra trips, and how American makes sure its new Europe flights have qualified crews. I wrote in April about American’s new Aggressive Pick-up system. It gives pilots access to last-minute open trips on a first-come, first-served basis. Those trips can come with premium pay. Junior pilots gained access to flying that senior pilots had been accustomed to getting. That helps American cover flights and creates opportunities for junior pilots. It also takes income opportunities away from senior ones. The fight over “fixing” the system is largely about who gets the money. The union wanted seniority to count in those awards, along with priority for pilots based where the trip originates and fixes to message delays. American saw something it could trade for. The union’s September 18 negotiating update described the exchange: Pilots would get changes to the extra-trip pickup system. Seniority and in-base priority would play a role, and the parties would address problems with how trip opportunities reached pilots. American would get changes to monthly schedule bidding for its Europe operation. The airline wanted Atlantic Europe qualifications incorporated into its Preferential Bidding System, the software that builds pilots’ schedules. The memo calls this an “A320” issue because that’s the pilot fleet category, which includes the A321XLR. A pilot qualified to fly an Airbus domestically still needs the additional qualifications for this oceanic flying. “AE” means Atlantic Europe here. American needs the pilots qualified for those trips to be available to fly them. A large pool of Airbus pilots doesn’t solve the problem if the pilots who can fly to Europe are awarded domestic schedules, while pilots who haven’t completed the necessary training are entitled by seniority to the Europe trips. The union’s October 27 update explained limited changes to bidding rules for Airbus pilots in categories with current or future XLR Europe flying, paired with seniority protections in the qualification training plan. Pilots discussing the proposed agreement described the risk of qualified pilots being directed toward Europe trips or reserve assignments they wouldn’t otherwise choose, while unqualified pilots could lose access to trips their seniority would otherwise let them bid. Pilots across the airline could benefit from changes to extra-trip awards, while the scheduling concessions would fall on the Airbus pilots affected by Europe flying. And restoring seniority in those awards helps senior pilots at the expense of junior pilots who’ve been quick enough to claim the trips. There’s a distributional problem inside the union. Some pilots argued that the union was giving up too much: American needed flexibility for an important expansion, and the union should obtain more for it in broader contract negotiations. The union had also filed a grievance over American’s failure to implement the Line Check Pilot program from the 2023 agreement, so training capacity was already a point of contention. American’s response is to divide the Philadelphia Airbus pilot group. It will reopen a domestic category and reduce the international category. A smaller, separately staffed international group gives American a more manageable pool to qualify and schedule for Europe. That avoids needing the rejected changes to keep the existing group together. The airline is using the base and displacement provisions in its contract. Under the pilot contract, reductions in a bidding category generally displace the least senior pilots, with provisions for more senior pilots to volunteer. Displaced pilots exercise their seniority into other positions, which can set off further displacement. A pilot can remain in Philadelphia on the same aircraft family but have access to different trips and schedules. Others’ choices could mean changing bases, aircraft, or commuting arrangements. American’s 2027 Europe plans include Philadelphia–Porto beginning March 28 and Philadelphia–Vienna beginning May 6, both using the A321XLR. I toured the aircraft before it entered service. It has just 155 seats: 20 business class suites, 12 premium economy seats, and 123 in coach. American can offer a premium product across the Atlantic with fewer seats to fill than on a Boeing 787. That opens up routes and seasons where a larger aircraft is harder to justify. I liked the operational benefit of making last-minute trips available to pilots willing to fly them. Getting an airplane out on time has value, and senior pilots losing priority for some extra income standing in the way of operational reliability has been a key cause of Delta’s operational meltdowns. Management calls the rejected deal objectively better. That depends on whose schedule and income you’re counting. A senior pilot seeking premium trips and a Philadelphia Airbus pilot facing restrictions on monthly bidding are different pilots gaining benefits and incurring costs. Much of a union’s role is trading off the same or better total benefits between its members, rather than getting the best possible overall deal from the employer. And union politics play an important role, especially as the American Airlines pilots union remains in the midst of drama over whether it will stay independent or join the larger Air Line Pilots Association. #5962. Three Women Argued Over An American Airlines Delay—Then Got Kicked Off And Blamed For Missed Connections

Three women were escorted off an American Airlines flight from Knoxville to Charlotte on Saturday night after an argument with a flight attendant, costing passengers their connections. Retired Kansas City Royals vice president Mike Swanson called them “princesses” in his story of the November 21 incident. The plane was already late getting to Knoxville, before the women could have held it up. Mike Swanson’s video of passengers being escorted off his flight — November 22, 2026 In a follow-up on Twitter, Swanson explains that one woman complained to the flight attendant about how long it had taken to board. The flight attendant told the women they were ready to depart and to fasten their seat belts. The exchange escalated: The three got loud and the attendant wasn’t having it. They gone. Video shows two women walking toward the front with their belongings, followed by a uniformed officer. Swanson says three were removed. He says several passengers missed connections in Charlotte. Yelling at a flight attendant because your flight is late is a lousy strategy for getting home sooner. Last year I wrote about an American Airlines passenger who told a flight attendant to shut up during the safety demonstration and wound up getting the plane sent back to the gate. It appears this was American Eagle flight 5675 on November 21, operated by PSA Airlines using a Bombardier CRJ900, registration N557NN. That flight was scheduled to leave Knoxville at 8:04 p.m. and arrive in Charlotte at 9:28 p.m. It took off at 9:57 p.m. and landed at 10:34 p.m. Charlotte is a particularly bad place to lose your connection buffer. I’ve written about how arriving on a regional jet can mean waiting for a valet checked bag and then making a long walk from Concourse E. A late evening arrival also leaves fewer chances to recover with another flight that night. However, that aircraft’s inbound flight from Charlotte didn’t land in Knoxville until 8:35 p.m. It was supposed to have arrived at 7:34 p.m. The plane was still arriving 31 minutes after it should have departed on its next trip. The women weren’t responsible for the original delay. Removing them may have used up whatever chance remained to make his connection, but we don’t whether he’d have made it without the argument. (HT: @bags) Topics on this pageAir travelAmerican AirlinesAmerican Eagle OutfittersBombardierBombardier CRJ900CharlotteKnoxvillePSA Airlines+6 more More From View from the Wing

Retired Kansas City Royals vice president Mike Swanson called them “princesses” in his story of the November 21 incident. The plane was already late getting to Knoxville, before the women could have held it up.

Mike Swanson’s video of passengers being escorted off his flight — November 22, 2026

In a follow-up on Twitter, Swanson explains that one woman complained to the flight attendant about how long it had taken to board. The flight attendant told the women they were ready to depart and to fasten their seat belts. The exchange escalated:

The three got loud and the attendant wasn’t having it. They gone.

Video shows two women walking toward the front with their belongings, followed by a uniformed officer. Swanson says three were removed. He says several passengers missed connections in Charlotte.

Yelling at a flight attendant because your flight is late is a lousy strategy for getting home sooner. Last year I wrote about an American Airlines passenger who told a flight attendant to shut up during the safety demonstration and wound up getting the plane sent back to the gate.

It appears this was American Eagle flight 5675 on November 21, operated by PSA Airlines using a Bombardier CRJ900, registration N557NN. That flight was scheduled to leave Knoxville at 8:04 p.m. and arrive in Charlotte at 9:28 p.m. It took off at 9:57 p.m. and landed at 10:34 p.m.

Charlotte is a particularly bad place to lose your connection buffer. I’ve written about how arriving on a regional jet can mean waiting for a valet checked bag and then making a long walk from Concourse E. A late evening arrival also leaves fewer chances to recover with another flight that night.

However, that aircraft’s inbound flight from Charlotte didn’t land in Knoxville until 8:35 p.m. It was supposed to have arrived at 7:34 p.m. The plane was still arriving 31 minutes after it should have departed on its next trip.

The women weren’t responsible for the original delay. Removing them may have used up whatever chance remained to make his connection, but we don’t whether he’d have made it without the argument.

#5961. Restored to Calder’s plan, the clouds are spinning again

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

Fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

“It’s totally phenomenal,” he said, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”

It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

Rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”

“It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”

It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

“We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he said. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”

Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

“We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how big this was until it showed up on their doorstep.”

Quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

“Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

“This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most important and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement said.

The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

“It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

But when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

“Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The new clouds, he said, are made of carbon fiber.

“These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

“I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

“I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he said, gazing up at it.

#5960. JD Vance Should Not Be Finger-Pointing in the Midst of War

The vice president ought to recognize the important role that diplomacy plays in a U.S. commitment to victory.

Vice President JD Vance speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Monroe, Mich., October 15, 2026.

President Donald Trump told Fox News’s Jacqui Heinrich that as for the Iranians who continue to find new ways to threaten Americans, “I’m going to finish it off — soon. One way or the other, we’ll finish it off.” In that same interview, he said he never liked the infamous Memorandum of Understanding, which gave the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps a cash infusion even as it continued firing on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The president has removed Vice President JD Vance, the face of and defender of the MOU, from leading negotiations with the Iranians, whom Vance claimed the U.S. had reformed. Weeks and dozens of attempts to kill Americans later, in response to Senator Tom Cotton’s questioning, National Counterterrorism Center Acting Director Joseph Weirsky told Congress what every American can see: “There’s no indication there’s any turning over of leaves with the regime.”

Vice President JD Vance speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Monroe, Mich., October 15, 2026.

Rebeccah Heinrichs is a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute and the director of Hudson’s Keystone Defense Initiative.

There is no shortage of choices for a cruise to the Caribbean — the most popular cruise destination in the world. More than 200 cruise ships spend at least part of every year in the region, and cruise-selling websites list thousands of individual Caribbean sailings.

This can be great news for would-be Caribbean cruisers, but it can also be overwhelming. With so many options, where do you even begin? Which one of these ships and sailings is the best?

We get the latter question a lot, and we always answer the same noncommittal way: It depends. The best ship and sailing in the Caribbean for whom? The best for us? The best for you? The best for your kids?

When picking the best cruise in the Caribbean, as with choosing the best cruise anywhere, a lot comes down to personal tastes and preferences. Some people love the big-resort feel of the biggest-of-big ships. Others are horrified by the very idea of them. Some people demand (and are willing to pay for) the highest levels of luxury. Others are on tight budgets. The best cruise for a family with kids isn’t necessarily the same as the best cruise for a couple looking for romance.

What kind of cruiser are you? It’s important to think that through before narrowing down your choices.

The bottom line is that the best Caribbean cruise for you depends a lot on your travel style. Below, we'll help you narrow your choices by looking at Caribbean cruises by category. The good news is that in the Caribbean, there really is something for everyone.

If your idea of a great vacation is a week at a big, bustling resort filled with every sort of amusement known to humans, you'll probably want to start your Caribbean cruise search with a look at the biggest vessels from lines like Royal Caribbean.

If "more is better" is your mantra, skip the search and look up Legend of the Seas, the newest of the Icon class ships.

At nearly 250,000 gross tons, the 20-deck-high vessel is among the world’s biggest cruise ships, alongside its sister ships Icon of the Seas and Star of the Seas.

Some of the wow factors on these Icon Class ships include massive water parks, cantilevered infinity pools, huge glass domes encompassing an indoor AquaTheater for acrobatic and diving shows, and innovative new cabin and suite layouts for families.

Legend of the Seas will depart Fort Lauderdale, Florida, on six-, seven-, and eight-night Western and Southern Caribbean itineraries.

Southern Caribbean sailings head to the ABC islands and stop at Perfect Day at CocoCay. Prices at about $1,509 per person, based on double occupancy.

Western Caribbean itineraries call at Costa Maya and Cozumel in Mexico as well as at Perfect Day at CocoCay. Prices start at $1,264 per person, based on double occupancy.

With at least two sea days per sailing, passengers will have ample opportunity to explore all the attractions the ship has to offer.

Related: Yikes, does Royal Caribbean’s new Icon of the Seas really cost that much?

In the family cruise arena, it’s hard to top Disney Cruise Line. As you might expect, the line caters heavily to families in every way, from onboard attractions to family-friendly cabin configurations.

Disney's special brand of magic translates just as well at sea. Kids receive the royal treatment with high-quality kids’ clubs and onboard attractions such as the 765-foot-long AquaMouse water coaster. Plus, there are plenty of chances for photo ops with their favorite Disney characters.

Parents will find opportunities to unwind at adults-only sundecks and pool areas that are closed to kids; there are also bars and clubs that are off-limits to anyone younger than 18.

Additionally, many cabins on Disney ships feature extra pull-down bunks and sofa beds, allowing four or even five people to stay in a single cabin. Most cabins have two bathrooms — one with a sink and a toilet, and the other with a sink and a shower or tub. This is rare in the cruise world, and it's designed to make it easier for families sharing a room to get ready.

For family fun on the high seas, try a seven-night Eastern Caribbean cruise aboard Disney Treasure. Departing from Port Canaveral, the ship stops in Tortola, British Virgin Islands; San Juan, Puerto Rico; and Castaway Cay, Disney's private island.

Sail on a themed cruise for Halloween or Christmas, and you can enjoy special onboard activities and events.

Prices for seven-night Caribbean sailings start at $3,648 for two people sharing a cabin.

Related: The ultimate guide to Disney Cruise Line ships and itineraries

When it comes to affordability, the undisputed leader in the Caribbean cruise market is Carnival Cruise Line. Not only does Carnival offer lower fares than you'll find at most rival lines, but it also purposely deploys its Caribbean-focused vessels to a wider variety of U.S. home ports than any other line. The idea is that a large percentage of the U.S. population can reach a Caribbean-bound Carnival ship by car, saving the cost of flights.

Related: The ultimate guide to Carnival Cruise Line ships and itineraries

Carnival ships are packed with fun-focused attractions, including multiple pool areas, water parks with waterslides, basketball courts, miniature golf courses and even roller coasters on select ships.

The cruise line is known for its multitude of included-in-the-fare dining spots. Every vessel has two main dining rooms and a casual buffet eatery. Most ships feature two of the best quick-serve poolside dining venues you'll find on mass-market ships at sea: BlueIguana Cantina for burritos and tacos, and Guy's Burger Joint.

Carnival ships sail to the Caribbean from all the major Florida cruise hubs but also from ports as far-flung as Baltimore; Norfolk, Virginia; Mobile, Alabama; New Orleans; and Galveston, Texas.

The line's seven-day Western Caribbean sailings from New Orleans on Carnival Liberty are a solid choice for budget-minded travelers seeking an affordable Caribbean escape from the middle part of America. Stops include the Honduran island of Roatan; Belize City, Belize; and Cozumel.

Rates for seven-day sailings out of New Orleans start at $444 per person, based on double occupancy.

Related: 6 ways to get a deal on a cruise

Looking to dip your toes into cruising for the first time, but not sure you'll love it? A great option in the Bahamas and Caribbean region is Margaritaville at Sea.

Founded in 2022, the Florida-based brand is particularly known for short and affordable sailings that offer the perfect entry to cruising for someone who isn't yet ready to commit to something longer and more expensive.

The line's original vessel, Margaritaville at Sea Paradise, operates out of West Palm Beach, Florida, with sailings as short as two days — an unusually short length in a market where most sailings are at least three nights or longer. These short two-night sailings start at just $189 per person, based on double occupancy.

At that length and price, even if you discover cruising isn't for you, you haven't committed all that much in time and money to figuring that out.

But you may very well find that you love it — particularly the sort of cruising that Margaritaville at Sea offers.

With its ships themed around the signature laid-back, Jimmy Buffett–inspired aesthetic that Parrotheads have come to love, the brand leans into a fun, social atmosphere (as the song says, "It's five o'clock somewhere"). It's more laid-back than the traditional party-focused vibe you find on some lines.

And should you eventually want to try a longer cruise, Margaritaville at Sea now offers those, too. In addition to two-night sailings, Margaritaville at Sea Paradise also operates three-, four- and five-night voyages out of West Palm Beach. The addition of a second ship in 2024 — the Tampa-based Margaritaville at Sea Islander — brought sailings as long as 10 nights.

Rates for four-night sailings out of West Palm Beach start at $149 per person, based on double occupancy.

When it comes to solo cruisers, the king of the hill in the Caribbean is Norwegian Cruise Line — at least, among the big-ship lines. In 2010, the Miami-based cruise operator began adding entire zones for solo travelers to the center of every new ship it deployed to the region.

You’ll now find these zones on Caribbean-focused vessels like Norwegian Encore, Norwegian Breakaway, Norwegian Getaway, Norwegian Epic and Norwegian Prima. Each of these solo cruiser zones, which are unrepeated in the industry for now, includes dozens of cabins for solo travelers, all clustered together. There is also a private lounge with a bar and a TV where solos can mingle at daily happy-hour gatherings.

Known as Studio cabins, the tiny solo rooms in these complexes measure just 100 square feet, but they're superbly designed to maximize storage space. The cabins' futuristic design and the multicolored mood lighting are particularly noteworthy.

Related: These 8 solo cruise cabins are great for travelers sailing alone

One big caveat about Norwegian's solo cabins: Most are interior rooms without an ocean view. Instead, they have windows overlooking a corridor. Another downside is that these cabins are so popular that they often sell out far in advance, sometimes at fares not much lower than fares for a cabin booked for two.

Single cruisers seeking rest and relaxation should consider the seven-night Caribbean sailings aboard Norwegian Luna, which depart from Miami.

The 3,550-passenger ship offers no shortage of restaurants, bars, late-night entertainment, comedy and slick theater shows, including the tribute show, "Elton: A Celebration of Elton John." Norwegian's freestyle dining is another boon for solo travelers. Rather than being locked into set dining times with strangers, passengers are free to dine with newfound friends at a time that suits them.

Norwegian Luna sails the eastern and western Caribbean on seven-night sailings out of Miami. Western Caribbean cruises also include a day at Great Stirrup Cay, Norwegian's private island in the Bahamas, which is home to the Caribbean's largest water park.

Rates for a Studio cabin start at $398 per person.

Related: The best credit cards for booking cruises

For those who wouldn’t be caught dead on a vessel that doesn’t have butler service and free-flowing caviar, the Caribbean can be a tough spot. Many of the world’s most luxurious cruise ships spend a lot of time in Europe and Asia or on round-the-world cruises. For some luxury lines, the Caribbean is almost an afterthought.

Luxury sailings in the Caribbean are also concentrated in the winter months, from December through March. Between April and October, options are much more limited.

However, if an upscale cruise experience is what you seek, Seabourn Cruises can deliver. The line's seven-day "Caribbean Gems" itinerary aboard Seabourn Ovation should be on your radar.

Seabourn specializes in small ships carrying fewer than 600 passengers. The line markets its vessels as luxury ships with a yacht-like atmosphere, while still offering familiar cruise-ship amenities, including indoor lounges and multiple restaurants and bars.

The 600-passenger Seabourn Ovation offers all-suite accommodations, with every suite featuring a private verandah. These range in size from 251-square-foot entry-level suites to the 1,306-square-foot owner’s suites.

Along with a lavish spa and fitness center, multiple pools, restaurants and bars, and a dedicated sushi bar, Seabourn Ovation offers butler service and the line's signature caviar service, available anytime, anywhere.

Rates start at $3,279 per person, based on double occupancy.

Virgin Voyages appeals to vacationers averse to the traditional cruising experience who crave a hip, party atmosphere. Ships are blissfully free of children — cruisers must be over 18 — making it a prime choice for an adults-only cruise.

Virgin has unique onboard offerings such as the first tattoo parlor at sea, numerous included dining options, free exercise classes and an app that lets you simply shake your phone to order Champagne (which can then be delivered just about anywhere on board). Fares also include all meals, soda and basic Wi-Fi.

Virgin's first vessel, Scarlet Lady, launched in late 2021, and the line has since added three more ships: Valiant Lady, Resilient Lady and Brilliant Lady.

Ships are filled with stylish, adult-oriented bars promising a hopping scene late into the night, as well as hipster venues like a colorful karaoke lounge. Onboard entertainment is inventive and often edgier than what you might see on traditional cruises.

Cabins sport a minimalist look with futuristic touches, and suites exude a rock 'n' roll vibe with in-room turntables and peekaboo showers.

The line's five-night "Dominican Republic and Bimini Beach Club" itinerary — which visits Bimini, Bahamas, and Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic — is available on multiple ships out of Miami and is a top option. With two sea days, the sailing offers a good mix of onboard activities and port-of-call exploration. Party by the pool or swim with stingrays during your day at Virgin Voyages' Bimini Beach Club. Chill out on a powder-white beach or go waterfall hunting in the jungle in the Dominican Republic.

Rates start at $695 per person, based on double occupancy.

Related: Virgin Voyages cruise cabins and suites: Everything you want to know

For couples wanting to dial up the romance, Windstar Cruises offers a more intimate way to explore the Caribbean. Its small, yacht-like ships cruise at a leisurely pace, anchoring off small islands and calling at quiet harbors far from the big-ship crowds.

Windstar specializes in small ships carrying between 148 and 342 passengers each. The line calls them yachts, but the ships are more like small cruise ships, with indoor lounges and communal dining rooms.

The line's seven-night "Classic Caribbean" itinerary aboard Wind Surf is a good choice for couples, with stops at some of the region's most appealing islands.

The five-masted vessel carries just 342 passengers and offers four types of accommodations, ranging in size from 188-square-foot cabins to 376-square-foot suites.

None has a private balcony, but the ship's open decks offer plenty of room to take in the views.

One of Windstar's biggest draws is its watersports platform, which opens at the stern when the ship is anchored and conditions permit. Couples can go kayaking or stand-up paddleboarding, swim in the sea or simply float in the water while taking in the views of a harbor dotted with yachts.

Back on board, Wind Surf has multiple dining venues, a pool, hot tubs, a spa and a fitness center. The ship's smaller scale also makes for a less crowded experience than you'll find on the big resort-style ships.

The seven-night "Classic Caribbean" itinerary begins and ends in St. Maarten. Expect sun-kissed beaches, secret coves and gin-clear waters in idyllic ports like St. Barts, St. Kitts and Nevis, Guadeloupe, Dominica and St. Lucia.

All-inclusive rates start at $2,922 per person and cover Wi-Fi, gratuities and unlimited beer, wine and cocktails.

#5958. American Airlines Loses O’Hare Gate Appeal—But United’s Plan To Drive It Out Of Chicago Is Failing

American Airlines just lost its appeal to undo Chicago O’Hare’s gate reshuffle. But it’s already bought two gates from Spirit, earned back gate space through its own growth, and survived United’s effort to push it out of Chicago. The airline’s position is stronger than when it sued, and judges haven’t finally decided whether the city broke its contract. The new ruling upholds the refusal to issue a preliminary injunction. The question of whether Chicago took American’s gates too early, after promising to give the airline a chance to grow into additional space first still hasn’t been resolved. I still think American has the better argument about the contract. I’ve also been skeptical from the beginning that they’d get an injunction, since money damages seemed possible. The November 19 appellate decision fits that distinction, although the trial judge’s preliminary reading of the contract was unfavorable to American. The judge accepted that Chicago made American an explicit promise The dispute goes back to the 2018 airport lease. United was getting gates freed up by Delta’s move to Terminal 5. American objected to widening United’s advantage, and Chicago agreed to three additional gates on the north side of the L concourse extension. The lease called for gate assignments following an attached map, with those assignments remaining in place for at least twelve months. American’s argument was that it needed to actually receive the promised capacity before that protected period could run. Otherwise United could grow using its additional gates while American waited for its own, and then the city would use the unequal flying to take gates away from American. The way gates work at Chicago O’Hare is that prior flying determines future gate space (or, technically, ‘linear frontage’). That’s the problem I identified when American first filed its lawsuit. The timing was part of the bargain that got American to support the redevelopment agreement in the first place. And the trial judget accepted that the city and American had agreed to tie the process to the three additional gates becoming operational: For purposes of this motion, that much—the Court has no doubt—was the deal. His position, though, is that the city’s fingers were crossed, suggesting that the explicit written commitment didn’t make it into the final lease, or at least that American couldn’t establish that it had: The language identifies completion of the Terminal 5 expansion and an airline’s relocation there as the triggers. It doesn’t separately name completion of American’s three gates. The additional gates appear on the map as common use space, which the city controls, rather than space reserved for American’s preferential use. The lease says it’s the complete agreement. The judge treated its language as unambiguous and excluded the earlier negotiations as a way to add a condition to it. American’s last additional gate became operational March 14, 2025. Under its reading, the protected year therefore ran through March 2026, and the next redetermination could begin April 1, 2027. Chicago instead treated the protected period as having begun in December 2023, allowing redistribution in 2025. The city’s reading is silly. The map is part of the signed agreement. Requiring the city to deliver the capacity shown there before starting a year of protected assignments doesn’t require inventing a promise outside the contract. And designating a gate common use doesn’t explain how a gate that isn’t operational can fulfill a promise intended to let an airline ramp up flying. Why American lost the injunction appeal The appellate court assumed American could satisfy the initial requirements for an injunction and still concluded that the harm from blocking the gate changes justified denying one. It was reviewing whether the trial judge abused his discretion, NOT deciding the contract dispute from scratch. American’s problem was that it didn’t establish losing the gates would destroy its Chicago hub. It planned to operate the same number of flights using fewer gates, with more flying at less attractive times and less room to recover from delays. That could cost money, make operations worse and harm passengers but it made the injury look measurable. That was my original point – that this would be a case for future damages rather than an injunction. Meanwhile, the other airlines had planned schedules around the redistribution. United projected more than 2,000 cancellations if it were blocked. That number was overblown but the court accepted that changing the arrangements would disrupt passengers, other airlines, and airport construction. And the expectation that American would win gates back in the next allocation (which it did) undercut the argument that it faced an irreversible decline. Timing hurt American, too. Chicago announced the redistribution in February 2025. American sued in May but didn’t request preliminary relief until July. By the September hearing, the October gate changes were imminent and preparations were well underway. American argued that the city shouldn’t get to invoke the hardships from correcting an agreement they deliberately broke. The appeals court rejected that approach because it saw a reasonable dispute over what the contract meant. In my view, Chicago (intentionally) muddied the contract issue enough to make it less clear. This decision doesn’t end American’s lawsuit. It upholds the denial of a preliminary injunction. The contract claims and potential damages are still unresolved. The court rejected the argument that implementation of the gate changes had made the appeal moot, since a court could still order an effective remedy. United’s strategy ran into the airport’s actual capacity Chicago seemed strongly inclined to help its hometown airline. United’s headquarters are valuable to the city, especially with rumors of a move to Denver hanging over the relationship. My coverage of the gate dispute even generated an angry phone call from Chicago “shadow mayor” Jason Lee. United saw a chance to turn American’s slow recovery from the pandemic into a permanent retreat. American had retired too many aircraft and couldn’t rebuild everywhere at once. Fewer Chicago departures meant fewer gates, which could make future growth harder. United CEO Scott Kirby tried to create pressure by talking up American’s Chicago losses and getting financial analysts to question why it should stay. United then announced additional flying on the morning of American’s earnings call, practically writing the questions for them. This was strategic flying. United clearly didn’t want all of that additional capacity. It wanted invesors to believe that any growth would be matched, so American couldn’t improve its gate position and would just lose more money trying. Kirby told analysts United would add “as many flights as are required” to protect its gate count. Then the Federal Aviation Administration intervened. The airport couldn’t handle the schedules airlines were filing, especially with construction constraining movement on the ground. Its summer order capped scheduled arrivals and departures at 2,708 per day from May 17 through October 24. The government used approved summer 2025 schedules as its baseline. It rejected rewarding airlines for filing unrealistic 2026 schedules to improve their negotiating position. United’s much larger proposed buildup didn’t entitle it to preserve that bigger share while forcing American to shrink. The government effectively called United’s bluff. The cap limited American, too, but it protected the existing competitive balance against United’s attempt to overwhelm it with additional flights. American had also grown enough during 2025 to earn back gate space in October’s redistribution. The returned space amounts to roughly three narrowbody gate equivalents. Separately, American acquired Spirit’s G8 and G10 gate leases for $30 million, which I was first to report. That reduces the practical stakes of this appeal, but it still seems that Chicago broke its agreement to benefit United. American needs Chicago to rebuild the business Kirby claims American loses so much money in Chicago that it should leave. Some version of those losses are real, created in part by the undersized schedule it had been flying. But the size and meaning of the losses get overstated. It requires assigning headquarters overhead to the hub that doesn’t disappear if the hub closes. And American would lose connecting traffic and credit card customers if that happened, too. American needs to be relevant in the largest markets where people spend heavily on cards. Retreating from Chicago would make AAdvantage less valuable to Chicago customers, and make its Citibank cards harder to sell and less attractive to spend on. Attributing credit card revenue to the customers and markets that generate it produces a different picture than spreading that revenue across flights throughout the network. That’s why Chicago belongs alongside American’s efforts to rebuild Los Angeles as gates return after construction, and its plans to bring Alaska Airlines into its Atlantic and Pacific joint ventures. They’re working to regain relevance in the largest spend markets in the country. The Chicago fight has also given employees something to rally around. In the post-earnings employee meeting I covered in January, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper called United the “common enemy” and made it out to be a battle for loyalty and credit card performance. He reported roughly 20% growth in loyalty enrollments, card acquisitions, and local market share over the preceding nine months. United’s much larger proposed buildup didn’t entitle it to preserve that bigger share while forcing American to shrink. The government effectively called United’s bluff.

The cap limited American, too, but it protected the existing competitive balance against United’s attempt to overwhelm it with additional flights. American had also grown enough during 2025 to earn back gate space in October’s redistribution.

The returned space amounts to roughly three narrowbody gate equivalents. Separately, American acquired Spirit’s G8 and G10 gate leases for $30 million, which I was first to report. That reduces the practical stakes of this appeal, but it still seems that Chicago broke its agreement to benefit United.

Kirby claims American loses so much money in Chicago that it should leave. Some version of those losses are real, created in part by the undersized schedule it had been flying. But the size and meaning of the losses get overstated. It requires assigning headquarters overhead to the hub that doesn’t disappear if the hub closes. And American would lose connecting traffic and credit card customers if that happened, too. American needs to be relevant in the largest markets where people spend heavily on cards. Retreating from Chicago would make AAdvantage less valuable to Chicago customers, and make its Citibank cards harder to sell and less attractive to spend on. Attributing credit card revenue to the customers and markets that generate it produces a different picture than spreading that revenue across flights throughout the network. That’s why Chicago belongs alongside American’s efforts to rebuild Los Angeles as gates return after construction, and its plans to bring Alaska Airlines into its Atlantic and Pacific joint ventures. They’re working to regain relevance in the largest spend markets in the country. The Chicago fight has also given employees something to rally around. In the post-earnings employee meeting I covered in January, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper called United the “common enemy” and made it out to be a battle for loyalty and credit card performance. He reported roughly 20% growth in loyalty enrollments, card acquisitions, and local market share over the preceding nine months.
