you almost think DL decided to get out of the central terminal and into terminal 5 not just to avoid the costs of the rebuild but also to set up this catfight between AA and UA.

It is also certain that AA failed to look down the road to realize it needed to protect its ORD gates – many of which it did not use because the aircraft were repositioned to its failed AUS experiment. But the judge is correct that the City of Chicago made enough promises and put them in writing that AA does have the basis for the case to keep going.

UA has failed at not only pushing AA out of ORD – AA’s revenue rehab efforts are going well enough that they can afford to selectively invest in what strategically matters – but also in preventing UA from building a megahub that it dominates as DL does at ATL and AA does at DFW and to a lesser extent CLT. The competitive environment at ORD is obvious from average fares that are $100 lower than DL gets at MSP and DTW and over $50 less than AA gets at DFW and DL gets at ATL. ORD is just a financial drag for both AA and UA.

this could have turned out much worse for AA but they have what they need to fight at ORD.

During my time living in the Chicago area from the 1980s through the late 2010s, I first started flying mostly with American. They were the first airline where I got a free family trip, mostly thanks to matching a promotion Midway Airlines ran. I was never a frequent enough traveler to keep my miles active, and they would frequently expire. In my later years in Chicago, I flew more on United, as it had better international options than American. AA didn’t fly to Paris, it’s flights to Tel Aviv were not as convenient, and their Asian options were limited. This put nearly all of my flying on United. I was almost never more than Silver, as all my flying was in the cheap seats.

To capture more passengers, AA needs more international flights from Chicago to both Europe and Asia, and they need more airplanes, and likely the new international terminal to provide more international gates. The international flights could bring them more relevance for both local travelers and connecting travelers to those flights. And this will cause those travelers to take more AA domestic flights, where the bread and butter of revenue comes from, as well as drive more revenue.

I don’t understand why Kirby uses a competing airline’s profitability as a rationale for trying to force them out of a market. He made similar comments when DL initiated, or reinitiated their HKG route.

Remaining in an unprofitable market is the airline’s and their Board’s decision.

Kirby loves press coverage but his ongoing rants only further hinders his credibility.

Perhaps his time would be better invested in improving his customers’ experience at the service level. An extensive route network is only one component of an airline’s reputation.

#5957. Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

“The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

At issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”

The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly said it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

“Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

“Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most important stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”

The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

“Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”

#5956. American Airlines Passenger Admits Taking Business Class Pillows—The Airline Calls It A Favorite Confession

An American Airlines passenger confessed to taking home two pillows from international business class. Their husband sleeps with one every night and can’t sleep without it. The second pillow is a backup. American told them it was delighted the pillows had found a loving home. That’s a very different reaction from United Airlines, which told flight attendants to stop passengers from taking its Polaris bedding. And I think American has the right instinct here. A passenger is still talking about how much they love the airline’s business class product a year after the flight. This is also an unusually good advertisement for an airline pillow. We have to admit… this may be one of our favorite confessions. We’re glad those pillows found such a loving home, and even happier to hear they’re still helping you both get a great night’s sleep! Thank you for sharing the laugh and for choosing to fly with us. — americanair (@AmericanAir) November 20, 2026 I Have Airline Blankets On My Couch On my couch at home I have American Airlines blankets from before the US Airways merger, along with Etihad first class blankets. The Etihad ones are some of the softest, most comfortable blankets I’ve ever used. They remind me of those flights, and make me want to get back on board. About a year ago, at American’s event introducing its Airbus A321XLR, I took home a 100th anniversary pillow. (With permission.) When my daughter was in preschool, parents sent their kids with sleep sacks for nap time. I sent her with a United Polaris cooling gel pillow. United actually sent me a cooling gel pillow in a promotional package in 2018. They understood the value of getting the product into someone’s home when it was their public relations team doing the sending. So it was even more odd to see passengers spending thousands of dollars with them as scoflaws. An airline can buy advertising to tell me its business class bed is comfortable. A blanket I actually use at home lets me experience a little of that comfort again. An unusual souvenir also gives someone a reason to ask about a trip. Now I’m telling the story of the flight, remembering what I liked about it, and introducing somebody else to the product. United Wanted Its Pillows Back. Holiday Inn Gave Away More Towels. In 2017, United told flight attendants to watch for passengers taking its new Saks Fifth Avenue bedding. all pillows and blankets are to be left on the aircraft at the end of each flight, including the cooling gel memory foam pillow. United said even a few missing items per flight could add up to millions of dollars across its network. They laundered and reused the bedding over multiple flights. The same instructions allowed passengers to take amenity kits, slippers and pajamas where offered. I argued that United should see the marketing opportunity. They’d finally developed bedding that customers actively wanted to bring home! There ought to be a way to take advantage of that enthusiasm. Holiday Inn did. Back in 2003, I wrote about its towel amnesty. The IHG brand declared August 28 Towel Amnesty Day and forgave guests who’d taken towels over the years. They didn’t just promise not to chase anyone. Their original announcement included more than 60,000 souvenir towels to give away, plus a dollar for Give Kids The World for every towel story collected. They turned missing inventory into stories about people’s stays. In 2013, Hyatt actively encouraged guests to take its bath amenities. Those little bottles could remind you of the hotel the next time you used them. That meant the toiletries supplied in your room, not clearing out a housekeeping cart. And it doesn’t translate into permission to remove today’s large communal shampoo dispensers. What a shame those germ farms are. Some Of The Best Airline Souvenirs Are Meant To Leave Airlines already know that small objects can become a reason to remember them, talk about them, and even book them again. KLM’s Delft houses. The airline gives miniature Dutch buildings filled with Dutch gin to intercontinental business class passengers. They’ve been doing it since the 1950s, and release a new house each year on their October 7 anniversary. There’s even an app to track your collection. The airline has given you something to collect on a future trip. Lufthansa’s rubber ducks. These began in the bathrooms of the Frankfurt First Class Terminal in 2004. Lufthansa’s own anniversary history describes delighted guests taking them home. The airline embraced it and created special editions. A little bath toy became a recognizable part of an expensive first class experience. Delta’s trading cards. You can ask a pilot for one. Delta says it distributed more than 3 million in 2024 and produced over 5 million for its 2025 collection. This works in coach, too. The souvenir comes with a conversation with a pilot. Other airlines offer these now, too. Virgin Atlantic’s salt and pepper shakers. The little aircraft-shaped shakers famously carry the words “pinched from” and “Virgin Atlantic” underneath. The airline has joked publicly about passengers taking them. They’ve made the souvenir story part of the design, although I’d still ask before pocketing tableware. Virgin Australia had a particularly good version of this: its business class salt and pepper shakers fit together to make the Sydney Opera House. Passengers took them home. A generic salt shaker doesn’t give you much to talk about. A tiny Opera House does. Amenity Kits Are A Marketing Deal, Too An amenity kit is supposed to go home with you. The toothbrush and eye mask help during the flight. A useful bag can stay in your life for years. I’ve written about the economics of these partnerships, including United’s Brooks Brothers kits. The brand supplying the toiletries or putting its name on the bag can be subsidizing the airline’s cost. That may mean free or discounted products, shared costs, or payments for exposure to premium passengers. In other arrangements the airline pays for a luxury name. The skincare company gets its product into the hands of someone who might buy it again. The airline gets a more desirable amenity and an association with the brand. Taking the samples home and finishing them is part of the point. Where I’d Draw The Line For passengers, the starting point is what you’re being given. Amenity kits and their contents, pajamas and personal slippers where offered, children’s activity kits, and souvenirs handed out by the airline are generally yours to keep. Bedding, mattress pads, reusable noise cancelling headphones, glasses, dishes and metal cutlery are generally equipment for use during the flight. Ask before taking them. For the airline, I’d be generous with a small, distinctive item that a passenger loves, provided it’s inexpensive enough to give away and there’s enough stock to keep delivering the promised product. Give employees room to say yes. There are clear limits. Hotel guests taking televisions is absurd. I’ve covered hotels reporting stolen mattresses. I’d ask for the pillow, take the amenity kit, and happily accept a commemorative gift like American’s anniversary cushion. If the airline wants its bedding back, selling it is another way to let the passenger keep the memory. United’s own shop lists a Saks Fifth Avenue duvet for $34 (currently out of stock, with more due November 27). That meant the toiletries supplied in your room, not clearing out a housekeeping cart. And it doesn’t translate into permission to remove today’s large communal shampoo dispensers. What a shame those germ farms are.

Airlines already know that small objects can become a reason to remember them, talk about them, and even book them again. KLM’s Delft houses. The airline gives miniature Dutch buildings filled with Dutch gin to intercontinental business class passengers. They’ve been doing it since the 1950s, and release a new house each year on their October 7 anniversary. There’s even an app to track your collection. The airline has given you something to collect on a future trip. Lufthansa’s rubber ducks. These began in the bathrooms of the Frankfurt First Class Terminal in 2004. Lufthansa’s own anniversary history describes delighted guests taking them home. The airline embraced it and created special editions. A little bath toy became a recognizable part of an expensive first class experience. Delta’s trading cards. You can ask a pilot for one. Delta says it distributed more than 3 million in 2024 and produced over 5 million for its 2025 collection. This works in coach, too. The souvenir comes with a conversation with a pilot. Other airlines offer these now, too. Virgin Atlantic’s salt and pepper shakers. The little aircraft-shaped shakers famously carry the words “pinched from” and “Virgin Atlantic” underneath. The airline has joked publicly about passengers taking them. They’ve made the souvenir story part of the design, although I’d still ask before pocketing tableware. Virgin Australia had a particularly good version of this: its business class salt and pepper shakers fit together to make the Sydney Opera House. Passengers took them home. A generic salt shaker doesn’t give you much to talk about. A tiny Opera House does. Amenity Kits Are A Marketing Deal, Too An amenity kit is supposed to go home with you. The toothbrush and eye mask help during the flight. A useful bag can stay in your life for years. I’ve written about the economics of these partnerships, including United’s Brooks Brothers kits. The brand supplying the toiletries or putting its name on the bag can be subsidizing the airline’s cost. That may mean free or discounted products, shared costs, or payments for exposure to premium passengers. In other arrangements the airline pays for a luxury name. The skincare company gets its product into the hands of someone who might buy it again. The airline gets a more desirable amenity and an association with the brand. Taking the samples home and finishing them is part of the point. Where I’d Draw The Line For passengers, the starting point is what you’re being given. Amenity kits and their contents, pajamas and personal slippers where offered, children’s activity kits, and souvenirs handed out by the airline are generally yours to keep. Bedding, mattress pads, reusable noise cancelling headphones, glasses, dishes and metal cutlery are generally equipment for use during the flight. Ask before taking them. For the airline, I’d be generous with a small, distinctive item that a passenger loves, provided it’s inexpensive enough to give away and there’s enough stock to keep delivering the promised product. Give employees room to say yes. There are clear limits. Hotel guests taking televisions is absurd. I’ve covered hotels reporting stolen mattresses. I’d ask for the pillow, take the amenity kit, and happily accept a commemorative gift like American’s anniversary cushion. If the airline wants its bedding back, selling it is another way to let the passenger keep the memory. United’s own shop lists a Saks Fifth Avenue duvet for $34 (currently out of stock, with more due November 27). Pan Am would hand out small carry bags to celebrities with the corporate logo. Back then, Hollywood stars would have their picture taken as they walked down the mobile stairs to the tarmac while arriving in Paris, London, or Rome to shoot a movie. Also, the airlines would have its name or logo just inside the exit door of the prop or jet for additional photo publicity. If in doubt, just Google photos of when the Beetles arrive at JFK in 1964; John Lennon has a Pan Am bag in his hand.

I have the blue thin Delta blankets ( turned them into rags ), red AA thin blankets ( my dogs sleep on them ), and the newish thicker UA blankets ( from my recent trip to HKG ). Up next: Cathay blankets on my Feb trip.

I still have one of those PanAm bags given to me when I bought a ticket in F to Tokyo at their NYC office back in the 70’s. That flight was on their 747SP nonstop.

What kind of low life rips off bedding from their flight.

Bunch of thieves on these planes. Explains a lot when you think about it…

Gotta love people who rationalize stealing.

Weird to take a biz class pillow, but if you really think that will change your life, I say go for it. AA is wise to play along. Better to get the brand endorsement than look like a cheap scold.

I have some really soft warm blankets from American international first class that were brought home years ago along with wine glasses from BA Concorde, Easterna and Pan Am first class and I treasure these wonderful souvenirs and wonderful memories.

When you pay $10K+ for a roundtrip to Europe, cash, then does it really matter?

Sure, the points people and hoarders are gonna hoard, but surely, it doesn’t even register a rounding error against $10K for 7 hours of flight time.

When UA first rolled out its Polaris bedding, I commented to an FA what a great travel pillow they had. The FA told me to take it if I wanted. I still use it a lot, and there is the association with UA as the cover is emblazoned with “United” and “Polaris”–a constant reminder and, to me, great marketing. Same with the pajamas. But they’ve cut back on everything, which I think is a mistake, especially with other airlines stepping up.

#5955. Deregulation Is Bringing Us Our First Nuclear Reactors of the Century

The Trump administration’s approach to cutting red tape is starting to pay off.

A rendering of the proposed Xe-100 nuclear reactor facility at Dow’s Seadrift plant in Texas.

Federal regulators have approved construction of four advanced nuclear reactors at a Dow chemical plant in Texas, the first approval of its type in 60 years and the next step in America’s red tape–free nuclear renaissance.

The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) issued a construction permit for the proposed plant featuring four Xe-100 small modular reactors (SMRs) at Dow’s Seadrift site in Texas — the first construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor issued in the U.S. in more than half a century. It’s the most recent sign that President Trump’s cutting of nuclear red tape last year is paying dividends.

Andrew Follett conducts research analysis for a nonprofit in the Washington, D.C., area. He previously worked as a space and science reporter for the Daily Caller News Foundation.

#5954. Etihad Launches U.S. Credit Cards With Elite Status—But Most Americans Should Skip Them

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Etihad has launched two U.S. credit cards, including a $499 card that offers Gold status after a single Etihad purchase. That’s the sort of benefit that usually gets my attention. But I wouldn’t recommend either card to most U.S. consumers.

Qatar Airways status that comes the first year with their premium card can get you into American Airlines and Alaska Airlines lounges on domestic trips (and American Airlines international business class lounge access). Emirates status lets you book first class awards that non-status members can’t. Etihad’s status doesn’t do either of those things, and you can earn their miles faster with other cards.

The two cards launched November 20 through First National Bank of Omaha. They’re Etihad’s first U.S. cobrands, with annual fees of $99 and $499.

Here are the main differences in the offers: Benefit   Etihad Guest Visa Signature   Etihad Guest Premier Visa Signature Annual fee   $99   $499 Initial bonus   40,000 miles: 10,000 after first purchase, plus 30,000 after $3,000 in spending within the first three billing cycles   60,000 miles: 20,000 after first purchase, plus 40,000 after $7,000 in spending within the first three billing cycles Etihad purchases   3 miles per dollar   5 miles per dollar Partner airline purchases   2 miles per dollar   3 miles per dollar Other purchases outside the U.S.   2 miles per dollar   2 miles per dollar Other U.S. purchases   1 mile per dollar   1 mile per dollar The initial offers require applying by February 3, 2027. Both cards waive foreign transaction fees. The Premier card also includes Priority Pass, a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fee credit every four years, and 3,000 miles after the first Etihad purchase and at each card anniversary. The status rules are: $99 card: Silver after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days. Keep Silver with $20,000 in annual card spending or $3,000 in Etihad purchases. $499 card: Silver at account opening, then Gold after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days. Keep Gold with $40,000 in annual card spending or $8,000 in Etihad purchases. Otherwise, you get Silver. Both earn one tier mile per dollar spent. The cheaper card caps this at 25,000 tier miles per calendar year, while Premier has no cap. These are status credits, separate from the miles you redeem for travel. So you can spend towards Etihad status. I like bonusing non-U.S. purchases, but if that’s meaningful to you then the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card is far better since it earns unlimited 3 points for every $1 spent on eligible foreign transactions. And I value Alaska’s miles far more than Etihad’s. But Etihad Gold Isn’t Qatar Gold When Qatar Airways launched its U.S. cards, the premium card’s first year of Gold status was immediately useful even to someone who never planned to fly Qatar. Qatar Gold is oneworld Sapphire. That means lounge access when flying American Airlines and Alaska Airlines, including domestic trips. It even gets you into American’s business class Flagship lounges on an eligible same-day itinerary. Etihad isn’t in an alliance. Their airline partnerships don’t turn Etihad Gold into an Admirals Club membership or give you those oneworld benefits on domestic American flights. The Premier card’s Priority Pass membership is a big nothingburger. Priority Pass is a drug on the market. Everyone offers Priority Pass. And Emirates gave its credit cards a purpose when it restricted first class awards to elite members. You need Silver status or higher to book a first class Classic Reward. You don’t need an Etihad card’s status just to redeem miles for the award you want. Etihad status can help when you actually fly Etihad, especially in coach. Lounge access and other benefits depend on your tier. But someone who mainly redeems miles for premium cabins already gets many of the things status would otherwise provide with their ticket. I’d Earn The Miles With A Different Card You don’t need an Etihad credit card to earn Etihad miles. Capital One, for instance, transfers to Etihad Guest at 1:1, and Venture and Venture X earn two miles per dollar on ordinary purchases. Citi and Bilt also offer transfers to Etihad. Put $40,000 of unbonused spend on the Etihad Premier card and earn 40,000 redeemable Etihad miles, while satisfying the spending requirement to keep Gold. Put that same spending on Venture X and earn 80,000 Capital One miles, which can become 80,000 Etihad miles. Or you can transfer them to a different airline. This is why I separate a card’s initial bonus and benefits from whether it’s worth using for spending. An Etihad bonus might help someone finish off an account for a specific award. That doesn’t make the card a good place to put their continuing spend. The narrow case I’d consider is someone who regularly buys Etihad coach tickets, will use the status benefits, and can retain Gold through $8,000 of Etihad purchases rather than diverting $40,000 of ordinary spending. For someone who wants Etihad miles for an occasional business or first class redemption, I’d earn transferable points with a better card. I wouldn’t pay $499 and give up half my everyday mileage earning just for Etihad Gold. Google Flights Explore is one of the best-kept secrets when it comes to finding cheap flights. You may have a basic familiarity with Google Flights in general, but once you know how to use Explore to find deals, it’s a whole other game.

It can unlock hundreds of dollars in savings for your next dream vacation.

Let’s dig deeper into the tool and how you can use it to plan your trips.

Google Flights Explore is a feature nested within Google Flights. You can gain access to it either by clicking the “Explore” button on the toolbar in Google Flights or by going directly to the Explore page.

Google preselects the location closest to where you’ve logged in (in my case, New York City). Then, it shows you the cheapest flights worldwide.

An interactive map lets you indulge your wanderlust. Whether you want to visit a nearby national park or see the Australian outback, the world is available at the click of a mouse.

If you know you want to get away on specific dates but don’t have a specific destination in mind, use Google’s open-ended search functionality to find flight deals within your window of availability.

Using Google Flights Explore is not complicated. Once you play with it a bit, you'll figure it out easily.

You can set your home base pretty much wherever you want. I mentioned that my search defaults to New York City, but for the sake of the examples below, I chose to search from Houston.

Google displays a highlights bar with a few popular destinations on the left side and an interactive map on the right. Clicking any of the cities pulls up the dates and prices; in this example, Google tells me that I can fly round-trip to Orlando for as low as $60 or to New York City for just $109. You’ll also see the lowest price Google finds for hotels on the left-side bar, next to the bed icons.

As you zoom out, the whole world opens up. Google tells me that, in this case, I can fly to Honolulu for $388 or to Tokyo for $895.

You can also move the map around to zoom in or out on a particular region that may strike your fancy.

But let’s say I had my eye on a trip farther afield — perhaps Paris. I can zoom in on Europe, and when I click the Paris pin, Google will show me flight options I can click to book on the traditional Google Flights page.

In this case, Google Flights Explore says that Paris is pricey from Houston at a whopping $987. That might have me looking at a getaway in London instead, where flights are as low as $692.

You also see that prices are currently “typical,” so there aren’t any screaming deals right now. I might hold off on booking in this case, but you see what a powerful tool this can be.

Google Flights Explore defaults to one-week trips within a six-month window, but you can change the parameters to search for other dates, including with its “Weekend” and “2 weeks” search options.

You can also click the “Specific dates” tab to enter exact travel dates and choose the number of passengers, cabin class (economy, premium economy, business or first class) and round-trip or one-way flights.

In this example, I’ve selected business class for a trip during Christmas (when I know I’ll be off work). Prices are pretty high right now, but the search could help me set up some flight alerts to monitor prices.

What if you’re looking to depart from a different overseas airport? Just put in the airport you want to travel from. In this case, I set my “home” city as Tokyo for a weekend trip in May; here’s what Google Flights Explore pulled up for me.

This could be helpful if, say, you’ve found a one-way award ticket to Asia but haven’t been able to find a good deal using miles to return.

You can also select specific airline alliances in Explore, but not individual airlines.

But there’s a way around it if you’re intent on a specific airline: Just start your search in traditional Google Flights, where you can select airlines. In this case, I chose only American Airlines. When I change the search destination to “Anywhere,” it only shows American flights on the Explore page. That’s a fun little hack.

As one more aside, you can conduct broader regional searches — such as Mexico or the Caribbean — if you’re targeting a general area but don’t know exactly where you want to go. Here’s an array of options from New York to the Caribbean; I’ve also selected the “Oneworld” filter to focus on American Airlines or other Oneworld partner flights. Flying to Barbados for $317 round-trip sounds good to me.

Here’s a similar search for Mexico from a home base in Seattle. I’ve eliminated any specific filters in this example to widen my options.

I like the sound of nine days in Cancun for just $378 round-trip. It even includes a hotel option for as low as $59 a night.

You can also use Google Flights Explore on your mobile phone. It functions nearly the same as the webpage version. In a search on my phone, I found flights from New York City to San Francisco for as low as $150 round-trip.

Google Flights Explore can also prompt you to select “When to visit” to triangulate the best weather and thinnest crowds.

We’ve touched on many of the most useful filters on Google Flights Explore, but aside from home airport, destination, number of passengers, one-way or round-trip tickets, class of service and dates, you can also click on “All filters” to view a litany of other options. These include the number of stops, “travel mode” (places available by car and plane or just by plane), price, destinations and the number of bags you can take. You can also search in various currencies and languages.

Once you go to Google Flights itself, there are even more options. In my searches, I tend to keep the filters unchanged to get the biggest picture possible — but, of course, your plans may vary.

Google Flights Explore can also help you plan your vacation. It’ll start by helping you pinpoint a destination with bargain flights; once you’ve decided on flights, you can use Google Flights Explore to find hotels as well. When you click on the hotel bed icon in your initial search, it takes you to a whole “Hotels” tab in Google (which deserves its own guide at some point).

I’ve stayed at the Hilton Cancun Mar Caribe All-Inclusive Resort — but at $504 a night, it seems pretty pricey. A better option might be the JW Marriott Cancun Resort & Spa, bookable via Priceline for just $319 a night.

Google Flights Explore is one of the handiest trip-planning tools out there. I’ve found it’s an invaluable research tool when I’m trying to figure out when and where to go; you can find cheap trips anywhere in the world by simply plugging in your home airport. By using it as a jumping-off point and triangulating with Google Flights itself, you’re sure to find the perfect vacation.

It’s a powerful tool and well worth investing some time exploring. Just be careful — it will no doubt also inspire wanderlust.

#5951. Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.

Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

“I think it’s outrageous,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking important.”

Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

"This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he said on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”

But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”

In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson said Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”

Johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he said.

There is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a plan in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

Senators on both sides of the aisle said they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

“I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability issue, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” said Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.
